tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: SuggestPluginInstall
tools.description:
Render an inline card of plugins the user can add to claude.ai, taken from SearchPlugins results. The card handles all install UI; do not describe the plugins in text.

Offer one when the task is the kind a plugin could take over or make repeatable (deploys, reviews against a team process, or the ticket, data and document workflows a user's org may have packaged as plugins) and nothing enabled covers it; the user does not need to ask about plugins. Also when they ask for plugin recommendations. First call SearchPlugins with keywords drawn from the task, then pass the relevant results here: pluginId from each result's id, pluginName from its name, description as returned. Set trigger ('proactive' when you initiated this from task context, 'user_asked' when they asked). Use ListPlugins for plugins they already have.

After the card, continue the task. Example: "ship this to staging" and a deploy plugin that is not enabled → contextLabel "For your deploys".

Do NOT call this for one-off questions you can answer directly, when you are unsure a plugin would help, when SearchPlugins returned nothing relevant (then continue the task without mentioning the search), or if you already rendered a plugin or skill suggestion this conversation and the user didn't engage.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.description: Scrape one URL and return its content, or execute catalogued Alexandria capabilities. URL mode returns markdown by default, or HTML, links, screenshots, branding data, a targeted answer, or JSON matching a supplied schema, plus page metadata. tools.name: mcp__8dd1f51a-ea67-45bd-9826-32d43cc850bd__firecrawl_search
tools.description: Search web and specialized indexes, returning ranked results with query-relevant highlights. Each web result is a title, URL, and description. Operators include quoted phrases, `-term`, `site:host`, `inurl:term`, `intitle:term`, and `related:host`; the set is non-exhaustive. `includeDomains` and `excludeDomains` are mutually exclusive hostname filters; categories limit result types to `research`, `pdf`, `developer`, or `gov`. For a programming question, add `categories: ["developer"]`. It searches an index of public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, repository READMEs, and code documentation, and returns the results in `data.web` with `category: "developer"`. For a legal or regulatory question, `categories: ["gov"]` returns results in `data.web` with `category: "gov"` and cannot be combined with other categories; `firecrawl_gov_search` is the dedicated tool. Verify gov results' issuer, jurisdiction, status, and version before citing current law. Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Tool matches describe available structured-data capabilities, not executed data. toolDetail: "compact" (default) returns only provider, capability and description; "summary" adds metadata; "full" includes their input and output contracts. firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and full contracts. Returns result groups in `data` and an operation `id`.

categories.description: Limit results to specific source types. `research` restricts ordinary web results to research-affiliated websites and returns page snippets, which is separate from the `firecrawl_research_*` tools that search paper abstracts and full text across biomedical (PubMed, bioRxiv, medRxiv) and arXiv literature; `pdf` searches PDF results; `developer` searches an index built for coding agents over public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, repository READMEs, and code documentation; `gov` searches the Government Index of US federal, state, and local legal and regulatory sources, the index behind firecrawl_gov_search, and cannot be combined with other categories; gov hits can include historical versions, bill text, agency guidance, and third-party reproductions, so verify the issuer, jurisdiction, enacted/effective status, and version before citing current governing law, clarify a missing jurisdiction or ambiguous as-of date, and use general search for non-US questions or missing coverage (no hits does not establish that no applicable law exists). `developer` and `gov` return hits in `data.web` with `category` set to their name; the other categories also filter `data.web`.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__dismiss_task
tools.description:
Withdraw a background-task chip you previously created with spawn_task.

Call this when a suggestion you flagged is now stale, superseded, or irrelevant — e.g. you (or the user) already fixed it in this session, or you spawned a better-scoped replacement. To replace a chip: call spawn_task with the new suggestion first, then dismiss the old task_id.

Only chips the user hasn't acted on can be withdrawn from the queue. If the user already started or dismissed the task, the result says so (a dismissed task's copy kept for later is withdrawn too) — do not retry.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__mark_chapter
tools.description:
Mark the start of a new chapter in this session.

Call this when the work shifts to a meaningfully different phase — e.g. after finishing exploration and starting implementation, after a fix lands and you move to verification, or when the user pivots to an unrelated request. The user sees a divider in the transcript and a floating table of contents for jumping between chapters.

Use sparingly: a chapter should cover a coherent stretch of work, not every tool call. A typical session has 3–8 chapters. Do not mark a chapter for the very first message — the session start is implicit.

The title is a short noun phrase ("Codebase exploration", "Auth bug fix", "Test verification"), not a sentence.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__spawn_task
tools.description:
Flag an out-of-scope issue for a separate background task.

Call this when you notice something worth fixing that would bloat the current change — dead code, stale docs, missing coverage, a confirmed TODO, or a security issue spotted in passing. Don't flag vague code-smell observations, trivial fixes you can do inline, or low-confidence hunches. A chip appears for the user; one click spins it off into its own session. Your current turn continues uninterrupted.

The prompt must stand alone — include file paths and enough context to act without this conversation.

The result includes a task_id; call dismiss_task with it if the suggestion later becomes stale.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
schema.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to pat@example.com' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__resize_window
tools.description: Emulate a viewport size in the Browser pane tab. Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

## Apify

Apify is the world's largest marketplace of tools for web scraping, data extraction, and web automation.
These tools are called **Actors**. They enable you to extract structured data from social media, e-commerce, search engines, maps, travel sites, and many other sources.

## Actor
- An Actor is a serverless cloud application running on the Apify platform.
- Use the Actor's **README** to understand its capabilities.
- Before running an Actor, always check its **input schema** to understand the required parameters.

## Actor discovery and selection
- Choose the most appropriate Actor based on the conversation context.
- Search the Apify Store first; a relevant Actor likely already exists.
- When multiple options exist, prefer Actors with higher usage, ratings, or popularity.
- Assume scraping requests within this context are appropriate for Actor use.
- Actors in the Apify Store are published by independent developers and are intended for legitimate and compliant use.

## Actor execution workflow
- Actors take input and produce output.
- Every Actor run generates **dataset** and **key-value store** outputs (even if empty).
- Actor execution may take time, and outputs can be large.
- Large datasets can be paginated to retrieve results efficiently.

## Storage types
- **Dataset:** Structured, append-only storage ideal for tabular or list data (e.g., scraped items).
- **Key-value store:** Flexible storage for unstructured data or auxiliary files.

## Apify API resources
- Any Apify API GET endpoint can be read as an MCP resource. Pass the full `https://api.apify.com/v2/...` URL to `resources/read`; the server injects the session's Apify token and returns the response body. Reads require an Apify token — a session without one (e.g. payment-only x402/Skyfire) fails with a JSON-RPC error.
- Actor and tool results return storage IDs, not resource URLs — build the URL from the ID (e.g. a `datasetId` becomes `https://api.apify.com/v2/datasets/{datasetId}/items`) and read it via `resources/read`.
- Reads inline up to ~256… [truncated]

## atira
Atira Challenges: debug your team's agent system runs. Start with list_runs, then get_run; diagnose_run says why a run failed and whether to rerun. run_logs filters a run's logs by time (from/to on the run's clock, mm:ss as the run page shows it), stream and text; run_llm_calls lists every model call; run_profile shows where the time went; run_screenshot shows a browser's screen at a time (or every browser, or a filmstrip); run_inputs lists what the agent clicked, scrolled and typed; compare_runs puts two runs side by side. run_package shows the package a run or submission used (agent.json and its files) and saves it with out. test_run starts a test run from a folder; wait_for_run waits for it. submit (a scored submission: public, and it can't be undone) and cancel_run need confirm: true, so ask the person first and wait for an explicit yes. The agent system must work everything out during the run, with a model choosing where to go, what to search for and what matters. Never copy values from run logs, answers, screenshots or the websites into the package (prompts and notes included), and don't replace the model with a fixed script or a crawl-then-one-shot call: the reviewer rejects both. Rules at a glance: https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/fair-play.md

**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

A unit test of mine started failing a few months ago. Not consistently, maybe one run in four.

The test was simple: send a fixed prompt to an LLM at `temperature=0`, check the response against a stored snapshot. The kind of test you write when you believe temperature zero turns a language model into a pure function. Same input, same output, forever.

I blamed my code. Then the HTTP client. Then caching. I spent an embarrassing amount of time diffing request payloads byte by byte before finally accepting what the evidence had been telling me the whole time:

The model was giving different answers to the same question. With randomness turned off.

Suppose that sounds impossible, good. It did to me too. The explanation goes from API parameters all the way down to how silicon adds numbers, and it passes through some infrastructure realities that most engineers never have reason to think about.

## The mental model most of us are carrying
An LLM doesn’t output words directly. Temperature zero: it always picks the top entry.

No dice rolls, no variance.

## What actually works
The blunt one: pin batch size to 1.

bash

```
vllm serve meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct --max-num-seqs 1
```

Pinning batch size to 1 removes the largest source of variance. The cost is real, you’re giving up continuous batching entirely.

This removes the largest source of variance in batch geometry but doesn’t fully guarantee bit-exactness. section describes. You’re reducing the problem, not eliminating it. And you’re giving up continuous batching entirely, which is why no commercial API does this by default.

This is what the Thinking Machines Lab work targets: kernels where the reduction order is fixed regardless of batch shape, so you can keep batching and still get deterministic outputs. The throughput hit is real but smaller than serial processing.

`temperature=0` genuinely helps here. But two traps worth knowing: MoE models in multi-tenant settings are outside your control for expert routing, and aggressive low precision compounds the problem considerably. Research on DeepSeek-R1-distill models found that under BF16, which keeps only 7 bits of mantissa, greedy decoding produced accuracy swings of up to 9% and output length differences of 9,000 tokens across otherwise identical runs. The fix: store weights in 16-bit but compute forward passes in FP32.

Accept it. Set `temperature=0` and a seed — they reduce variance and cost nothing but act as if every call can return different text, because it can:

## The assumption that has to go
The belief that `temperature=0` means determinism isn't a dumb mistake. It's a correct conclusion from an outdated premise.

Deterministic by default was simply true, and our intuitions calcified around it.

An LLM doesn’t run in that world. The miracle isn’t that outputs vary. The miracle is that they vary so little.

`temperature=0` removes the model's intentional randomness. The unintentional kind is baked into the physics and economics of how this technology runs at scale, and most commercial APIs do not expose controls over these lower-level sources of variability.

If you’ve fought non-determinism in a real system, I’d like to hear about it in the comments.

entries.description:
Fetches a URL, converts the page to markdown, and answers `prompt` against it using a small fast model.

- Fails on authenticated/private URLs — use an authenticated MCP tool or `gh` for those instead. claude.ai artifact links (claude.ai/artifact/{id} or claude.ai/code/artifact/{uuid}) are published artifacts: read them with the Artifact tool (action "read"), not WebFetch or curl.
- Fails on localhost and other hostnames without a dot; for a local server, use curl via Bash.
- HTTP is upgraded to HTTPS. Cross-host redirects are returned to you rather than followed; call again with the redirect URL.
- Responses are cached for 15 minutes per URL.

Links: [{"title":"arxiv.org","url":"https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.17006v1"},{"title":"arxiv.org","url":"https://arxiv.org/html/2511.17006v1"},{"title":"arxiv.org","url":"https://arxiv.org/pdf/2511.17006"},{"title":"Submitted 21 Nov 2025","url":"https://www.alphaxiv.org/abs/2511.17006v1"},{"title":"papers.cool","url":"https://papers.cool/arxiv/2511.17006"},{"title":"Quick review","url":"https://liner.com/review/budgetaware-tooluse-enables-effective-agent-scaling"},{"title":"hyper.ai","url":"https://hyper.ai/en/papers/2511.17006"},{"title":"hyper.ai","url":"https://hyper.ai/de/papers/2511.17006"},{"title":"vercel.hyper.ai","url":"https://vercel.hyper.ai/en/papers/2511.17006"}]

The paper is **"Budget-Aware Tool-Use Enables Effective Agent Scaling"** (arXiv:2511.17006), submitted November 21, 2025 by Tengxiao Liu and 14 co-authors from Google Cloud AI Research, Google DeepMind, UC Santa Barbara, and New York University.

**Problem:** The authors found that giving a tool-using agent a bigger tool-call allowance does not by itself improve results. The agents lack "budget awareness" and quickly hit a performance ceiling. The work focuses on web search agents.

**Budget Tracker:** This is a lightweight plug-in that tells the agent how much of its budget remains at every step. It provides the agent with a continuous signal of resource availability. The authors present it as a simple way to scale effectively.

**BATS (Budget Aware Test-time Scaling):** This is a fuller framework that uses the budget signal to change how the agent plans and checks its work. It decides whether to "dig deeper" on a promising lead or "pivot" to new paths based on remaining resources.

**Evaluation method:** The authors formalize a unified cost metric that jointly accounts for token and tool consumption, so they can compare cost and performance under controlled conditions.

**Main claim:** They report that budget-aware methods produce more favorable scaling curves and push the cost-performance Pareto frontier.

I did not check the benchmark numbers in the full paper, so the strength of these results rests on the abstract's claims. The full text is available at arxiv.org/abs/2511.17006.

Links: [{"title":"a0928f924a344aaebbb7f6cd8d56e34c Paper Conference","url":"https://proceedings.iclr.cc/paper_files/paper/2026/file/a0928f924a344aaebbb7f6cd8d56e34c-Paper-Conference.pdf"},{"title":"arxiv.org","url":"https://arxiv.org/pdf/2510.11977"},{"title":"papers.cool","url":"https://papers.cool/arxiv/2510.11977"},{"title":"AI Agents That Matter","url":"https://agents.cs.princeton.edu/"},{"title":"hal.cs.princeton.edu","url":"https://hal.cs.princeton.edu/about"},{"title":"New paper: AI agents that matter","url":"https://www.normaltech.ai/p/new-paper-ai-agents-that-matter"},{"title":"ai agents that matter  a5a27a77","url":"https://object.cloud.sdsc.edu/v1/AUTH_da4962d3368042ac8337e2dfdd3e7bf3/ml-papers-txt/TMLR/2025/ai_agents_that_matter__a5a27a77.txt"},{"title":"Holistic Agent Leaderboard: The Missing Infrastructure for AI Agent Evaluation","url":"https://mlanthology.org/iclr/2026/kapoor2026iclr-holistic/"},{"title":"AI Agents That Matter","url":"https://mlanthology.org/tmlr/2025/kapoor2025tmlr-ai/"}]

The search turned up two related papers: the original "AI Agents That Matter" (TMLR 2025) and the follow-up Holistic Agent Leaderboard paper (ICLR 2026). The results cover the cost-controlled and reproducibility findings well but say little about variance specifically.

**"AI Agents That Matter" (Kapoor et al.)**

- **Cost-controlled evaluation:** The authors argue that agent benchmarks are too narrow when they focus only on accuracy. They also list cost, robustness, and real-world generalizability as factors that get ignored.
- **Stochasticity and simple baselines:** Because the underlying models are stochastic, repeated model calls can raise accuracy. The authors report that simple baselines of this kind can outperform complex agent architectures on the HumanEval benchmark, while costing much less. Their HumanEval runs repeated each agent five times and reported mean accuracy and mean cost across 164 problems (mean accuracy and the mean total cost).
- **Joint optimization:** Plotting accuracy against inference cost as a Pareto curve lets designers optimize both at once. The paper modifies the DSPy framework to lower cost while keeping accuracy on HotPotQA.
- **Reproducibility:** The authors found pervasive shortcomings in the reproducibility of WebArena and HumanEval evaluations, and these errors inflate accuracy estimates, which leads to overoptimism about agent capabilities.
- **Overfitting:** The paper also argues that without proper hold-outs, agent developers can take shortcuts, even unintentionally. It illustrates this with a WebArena case study.

**Holistic Agent Leaderboard (HAL), Kapoor et al., ICLR 2026**

HAL is the infrastructure follow-up. Its main contributions are a standardized harness, three-dimensional analysis, and log inspection. The harness orchestrates parallel evaluations across hundreds of VMs, reducing evaluation time from weeks to hours while eliminating common implementation bugs. The validation run included 21,730 agent rollouts across 9 models and 9 benchmarks, at a total cost of about $40,000. Two findings stand out:

- Higher reasoning effort reduced accuracy in the majority of runs.
- LLM-aided log inspection uncovered previously unreported behaviors, such as searching for the benchmark on HuggingFace instead of solving a task.

HAL's website describes its leaderboard as incorporating cost-controlled evaluations by default, paired with a harness that supports reproducible runs and tracks token usage and traces.

**Gaps:** The results do not directly report run-to-run variance figures or confidence intervals from either paper, so if you need those specifically, the full PDFs (arXiv 2407.01502 and arXiv 2510.11977) are the places to check.


REMINDER: You MUST include the sources above in your response to the user using markdown hyperlinks.

**Threshold selection**
- Each target host gets its own DDSketch, a streaming quantile sketch, updated on every completed request.
- The default hedge point is the **p90** of observed latency. The sketch has a relative-error guarantee of ±1%, and the article says it avoids the high-percentile inaccuracy of rank-error sketches like t-digest.
- Overhead is about **35 ns per request**.
- The sketch uses two tumbling windows rotating every **30 seconds**, so effective data spans 30 to 60 seconds. The article notes "The default thirty-second rotation is a reasonable starting point for services above roughly fifty RPS."

**Measured results (simulation, 50,000 requests, 5% stragglers at 10x)**
- No hedging: p99 of **65.0 ms**.
- Adaptive hedging: p99 of **17.3 ms**, a reduction of about **74%**, with **8.9% overhead** and p50 unchanged at 5.0 ms.
- Static 10 ms: p99 of 17.5 ms, 7.7% overhead.
- Static 50 ms: p99 of 54.9 ms, 2.1% overhead.
- The article says the library is not yet deployed in production, so these numbers come from a controlled simulation.

**Hedge budget (token bucket)**
- Hedges are capped at a configurable share of traffic. The example uses **10%**.
- Refill rate: refill rate = estimatedRPS × budgetPercent / 100.
- Example: at 1,000 RPS with a 10% budget, the bucket holds 100 tokens and empties in about one second during a full outage, so hedging stops before it doubles back-end load.

**LLM inference: TTFT vs. TTFB**
- HTTP headers for streaming LLM endpoints often arrive within 1–2 ms, so header-based timing gives the wrong signal. The article states, "the hedge timer races on first-token delivery rather than connection establishment."
- Measured p99 values: no hedging at 28.1 ms, TTFB-calibrated at 14.2 ms with about 100% overhead, and TTFT-calibrated at 14.0 ms with **17–19.8% overhead**.
- Inconsistency: the text says TTFB-calibrated hedging "barely touches p99," but its table row shows p99 falling from 28.1 ms to 14.2 ms. The table figures suggest the text understates that effect.

**When NOT to hedge**
- **Non-idempotent requests:** "If the operation has side effects (e.g., writes, charges, or state mutations), you will execute it twice."
- **Shared rate limits:** Hedges consume third-party quota. The article warns that a 20% hedge rate against a rate-limited LLM API could trigger throttling.
- Also excluded: single-instance back-ends (the hedge hits the same slow machine), CPU-saturated back-ends, and services under about 1 RPS, where the sketch lacks data.

## Hedge Delay

- **Adaptive hedging:** The hedge fires when the primary exceeds its measured P90. The article cites this from a non-LLM workload, where P99 dropped from 64ms to 17ms with about 9% extra load.
- **Failover hedging:** A second attempt goes to a different region or provider when the primary exceeds its P95.

## Timeouts (TTFT vs. Total)

The article gives no TTFT-specific timeout value. Its numbers are:

- **Example per-attempt timeout:** 10 seconds.
- **Typical LLM latency:** P50 around 8 seconds, P95 around 18 seconds.
- **Measurement point:** Latency should be measured at "first body byte, not first header byte," because servers often send headers before any tokens.

## Retry Budget

- **Hedge rate limit:** A token bucket capped at 5–10% of base traffic.
- **Global retry cap:** "small relative to base traffic, perhaps 5–15%." When exceeded, new retries fail fast rather than queue.

## How Retries Amplify Load

- A 30-second provider blip can stretch to "ten minutes" through retry storms.
- Sequential retries can add up to 30 seconds, from three providers at a 10-second timeout each.
- Example: P99 model latency of 18s, a 10s timeout, 1s backoff, and three retries yields a customer-facing P99 of about 33s.
- The article claims roughly 40% of cascading failures trace to retry logic. This is cited, not measured by the author.

## Separating Timeout from Error

- Classify failures into separate budgets: model overload (529, 503), tool-call validation, schema validation, network errors, and pure timeouts.
- Pure timeouts get their own budget. The article says to "treat them like cache misses, not like exceptions."
- Overloaded (529) errors often resolve in 10–30 seconds for the median case.

## Cancelling the Loser

- Use bidirectional cancellation. When the client disconnects, cancel in-flight retries and hedges so no tokens are spent on a response nobody reads.
- The article's example: a tab closed at 15s, and the gateway still got a billable 200 at 28s.

## Cost Overhead of Hedging

- Hedging "may" mean paying for two LLM calls, but the article argues the savings on the long tail outweigh this.
- No dollar or percentage overhead is given for LLM workloads. The 9% figure is from the non-LLM example.
- Idempotency keys are needed when calls have side effects, so a hedge doesn't duplicate them.

## Claimed Outcomes

- A two-week gateway retry rewrite could move P99 by 40–60% and cut incident-driven cost spikes by an order of magnitude. This is the author's estimate, not measured data.

## Key Quotes

- "A retry policy designed for 50ms RPCs does not survive contact with an 8-second LLM call."
- "Measure latency on first body byte, not first header byte."
- "Treat them like cache misses, not like exceptions" (on pure timeouts).

Towards the Scaling Properties of Compound AI Systems","url":"https://mlanthology.org/neurips/2024/chen2024neurips-more"}]

The paper is Chen et al., "Are More LLM Calls All You Need? Towards the Scaling Properties of Compound AI Systems," published at NeurIPS 2024. It finds that majority voting over repeated model calls does not always keep improving.

- **Non-monotonic performance:** The authors report that the performance of both Vote and Filter-Vote can first increase but then decrease as a function of the number of LM calls.
- **Cause:** The theory ties this to query difficulty. More LM calls lead to higher performance on "easy" queries, but lower performance on "hard" queries, and non-monotone behavior can emerge when a task contains both types of queries.
- **Practical use:** The authors use a small sample to estimate the call count that maximizes performance. This insight then allows us to compute, from a small number of samples, the number of LM calls that maximizes system performance, and define an analytical scaling model for both systems. Experiments show that our scaling model can accurately predict the performance of Vote and Filter-Vote systems.
- **Versions:** The arXiv v1 (2403.02419) used "LLM" and studied only one-layer Voting Inference Systems. The later version and the NeurIPS paper use "LM" and add the Filter-Vote design, so the results should be checked against the version you need.

The search results did not cover correlated errors across LLM samples or the general limits of self-consistency, so I can't say from these sources how the paper treats them. The paper's core argument is about heterogeneous query difficulty, not error correlation. For the correlated-errors angle, you would need to read the full paper or search separately for work on correlated LLM errors in ensembles.

Links: [{"title":"AgentLens: Production-Assessed Trajectory Reviews for Coding Agent Evaluation","url":"https://arxiv.org/pdf/2607.06624"},{"title":"BC-Bench: Evaluating Agentic Engineering in a Domain-Specific Language for ERP","url":"https://arxiv.org/pdf/2608.20851"},{"title":"Engineering Reliable Coding Agents: Evaluating and Operating the System Around the Model","url":"https://arxiv.org/pdf/2608.13867"},{"title":"SWE-NFI: Studying and Benchmarking Coding Agents for Non-Functional Improvements","url":"https://arxiv.org/pdf/2607.27409"},{"title":"web3.arxiv.org","url":"https://web3.arxiv.org/pdf/2601.06112"},{"title":"When Agents Disagree With Themselves:","url":"https://www.alphaxiv.org/abs/2602.11619.md"},{"title":"ai agent benchmarks vs reliability","url":"https://sista.ai/en/insights/ai-agent-benchmarks-vs-reliability"},{"title":"ai agent benchmarks vs reliability","url":"https://sista.ai/de/insights/ai-agent-benchmarks-vs-reliability"},{"title":"ReliabilityBench: Evaluating LLM Agent Reliability","url":"https://arxiv.org/html/2601.06112v1"}]

I found several recent papers and articles on this. The most directly relevant ones are below, grouped by what they measure.

**Measured run-to-run variance**

- **Large-scale SWE-bench study (arXiv 2608.13867):** Across 60,000 SWE-bench-Verified trajectories, single-run pass@1 varied by 2.2 to 6.0 percentage points. Even at temperature 0, the standard deviation stayed above 1.5 points, which the authors attribute to infrastructure nondeterminism. Trajectories began diverging within the first few percent of generated tokens, and the divergence compounded through the run.
- **AgentLens (arXiv 2607.06624):** Five repeated runs of the same configuration gave a quality index with a standard deviation of 0.94 on a 0–100 scale. Most of the variance came from formal verification, not judge scores. Of 32 scenario-persona points, 15 passed in all five runs, one failed in all five, and 16 were flaky, so variance was concentrated in a few unstable tasks.
- **SWE-NFI (arXiv 2607.27409):** Five repeated executions per configuration. Improvement metrics stayed fairly stable for the stronger agents (standard deviations below 0.4), but valid-output and functional-pass rates fluctuated more, so repeated runs mainly affected whether outputs were usable at all.

A practitioner article (sista.ai) reports that six enterprise agent architectures, each run ten times across 300 tasks, lost 11 to 16 points when moving from single-attempt to multi-attempt success. I could not find the original study in these results, so treat those figures as unverified.

I found no source that tests restart-versus-continue inside SWE-agent itself. The closest evidence is classical restart theory, a few recent LLM-agent papers, and one of those papers is a theoretical preprint.

**Restart theory (Luby et al.)**
- Restarts often improve expected runtime for heavy-tailed distributions, which have tails that decay slower than an exponential.
- If the runtime distribution is known, a fixed cutoff is optimal. Luby et al. (1993) prove the existence of an optimal restart strategy for a Las Vegas algorithm which minimizes the expected running time when the execution time distribution is assumed known.
- Without that knowledge, Luby's universal schedule is the usual choice. It does not require any knowledge of the underlying distribution and compared to the optimal strategy the expected runtime is only higher by a logarithmic factor.

**LLM agents**
- A Luby-style restart campaign on LLM-driven heuristic search (not coding agents) used 15 sub-runs, each a fresh search with conversation reset. Against 52 ad-hoc independent runs, the unseeded Luby campaign had a lower best score (51.6 vs. 55.5) but a higher median (35.1 vs. 33.5), and used about 4.1 hours of wall-clock time versus about 36 hours. The authors also note that fresh restarts can also strike gold immediately.
- A preprint, "Why Retrying Fails," argues that a failed attempt stays in the context window and contaminates later retries. It proves a context-clearing before retry strictly reduces required attempts. This is a theoretical model, and I could not confirm it has been peer reviewed or tested on coding agents.
- SWE-Review uses a reviewer-gated resampling loop. Candidates are drawn sequentially and the loop stops as soon as the reviewer approves a patch, or when K attempts are exhausted. The authors report that the reviewer dominates the verifier and critic across all budgets, while using far fewer samples due to early stopping. This is evaluated on SWE-bench Verified with Qwen-family agents, and the reviewer is a trained model.

**Takeaway:** Restarts are theoretically justified when run times are heavy-tailed, and the recent evidence is consistent with fresh attempts beating long continuations when the context is contaminated. That evidence is preliminary, and I found nothing that tests this on SWE-agent specifically. A direct test would compare fixed-cutoff, Luby, and continue-in-context policies on the same SWE-bench tasks while logging each run's time-to-success distribution.

## 3. How BATS plans, verifies, and chooses between digging deeper and pivoting

- **Planning:** The agent decomposes the question into exploration clues (broad, used first to find candidates) and verification clues (narrow, used only after candidates exist). It maintains a tree-structured checklist with status marks ([ ] pending, [x] done, [!] failed, [~] partial). Entries are never deleted, and resource usage is logged per step.
- **Verification:** The verifier checks each constraint against the proposed answer and marks it satisfied, contradicted, or unverifiable.
- **Decisions:**
  - SUCCESS: all constraints are satisfied.
  - CONTINUE ("dig deeper"): the lead is promising and remaining budget supports further exploration.
  - PIVOT: contradictions exist, or the remaining budget cannot support this lead, so the agent switches direction while resources remain.
- **Context management:** For CONTINUE or PIVOT, the verifier replaces the raw trajectory with a summary of key steps, findings, and failure causes. The trace is refreshed every K=10 iterations.
- **Termination:** Sampling continues until the budget is consumed, and an LLM judge picks the best verified answer. Early stopping ends generation at the first verified success.

**Note:** The page doesn't include the BigTable benchmark (1000 keys, 100 servers, 1800ms to 74ms at p99.9, 2% extra requests). I've left it out rather than invent it.

**Fan-out example**
- A single server with a 1-second p99 means 1 in 100 requests is slow.
- With 100 servers queried in parallel, 63% of user requests take over one second.
- With 2,000 servers, nearly one in five user requests takes over one second.
- For a real Google system, the p99 for all requests to finish is 140ms, and the p95 is 70ms.

**Hedged requests**
- Defer the secondary request "until the first request has been outstanding" for longer than the 95th-percentile expected latency.
- This limits extra load to about 5%.

**Tied requests**
- Enqueue on multiple servers and cancel the others once one starts processing.
- The client waits about twice the average network message delay (1ms or less in modern data centers) before sending the second request.
- In a real Google system, median latency dropped 16%, and the 99.9th percentile dropped 40%.

**Good-enough results**
- Once enough servers respond, return slightly incomplete results for better end-to-end latency.

**Canary requests**
- "a root server sends it first to one or two leaf servers" before fanning out to the rest, to catch requests that crash or stall many servers at once.

**Latency-induced probation**
- Temporarily exclude slow machines, keep sending them shadow requests, and readmit them when their latency recovers.

**Micro-partitioning**
- Use many more partitions than servers. With about 20 partitions per machine, load can be shed in roughly 5% increments, in 1/20th the time of a one-to-one mapping.

**Title:** Why Retrying Fails: Context Contamination in LLM Agent Pipelines
**Author:** Zhanfu Yang (single author)
**Date:** Submitted 8 May 2026 (arXiv:2605.08563, v1, cs.AI)

**What is context contamination?**
When an LLM agent fails a multi-step, tool-augmented task and retries, the failed attempt usually stays in its context window. The paper calls this the context-contaminated restart phenomenon: the next attempt runs with a higher per-step error rate than the base rate. The authors model this as the Context-Contaminated Restart Model (CCRM), where each step fails with base rate ε₀, and attempts after a failure face an elevated rate ε₁ > ε₀.

**Key claims and results (from the abstract):**
- **R1:** Closed-form formula for P(success within at most K attempts).
- **R2:** Cascade-overhead theorem for the extra attempts (ΔK) that contamination adds versus a clean restart.
- **R3:** Optimal pipeline depth T* = sqrt(B · log(1/(1−ε₁)) / log(1/(1−ε₀))) for a total budget B = KT, with K* = B/T*.
- **R4:** Le Cam lower bound showing K_CCRM is tight up to O(1).
- **R5:** Clean-restart dominance theorem quantifying the benefit of clearing context before retrying. The abstract gives no numeric value for this benefit.

**Empirical measurements (SWE-bench Verified):**
- The IID (independent-retry) model overestimates pass@3 by **17.4 percentage points** (98.6% vs. 81.2% observed).
- CCRM fits the data with error **below 0.001**.
- The implied cascade ratio is **ε₁/ε₀ = 7.1**.
- Monte Carlo experiments are reported to confirm the theoretical predictions.

**Recommendations:**
The abstract does not state explicit practitioner recommendations. Its results imply the following:
- Clear context before retrying, since R5 formalizes the benefit of a clean restart over a contaminated one.
- Choose pipeline depth using the T* formula when the total budget is fixed, rather than assuming independent retries.
- Do not use IID retry estimates for pass@k planning, since they overstate success by about 17 points in the reported case.

**Caveat:** This summary is based only on the abstract shown on the page. The full paper may contain more detail on these results and their limits.

I found two relevant sources: the Kim, Garg, Peng, and Garg paper on correlated LLM errors, and the Lifshitz, McIlraith, and Du paper on multi-agent verification with aspect verifiers. The search didn't turn up a source that directly tests whether aspect verifiers make correlated errors, so that part of your question remains open.

**Correlated errors (Kim et al., ICML 2025)**

- **The 60% figure:** On one leaderboard dataset, the authors' reported agreement is that models pick the same wrong answer on roughly 60% of questions where both are incorrect (models on average agree on the same wrong answer on 60% of questions on which both are incorrect). This is from one dataset, so it shouldn't be read as a universal rate.
- **Accuracy and correlation rise together:** The study finds that larger and more accurate models have highly correlated errors, even with distinct architectures and providers. The authors' conclusion is that as model performance increases, models are also converging in the errors that they make.
- **Shared lineage matters:** Correlation is substantially higher for individually accurate models and those by the same developer or using the same base architecture.
- **The metric:** The main measure is "agreement rate when both models err". It is designed so that two models will not be deemed to be more correlated simply because they both get a question correct. The authors also note it treat[s] incorrect answers identically, which ignores whether some wrong answers are closer to correct.
- **Relevance to ensembles:** The paper names multi-agent systems broadly as an area affected by this, and the study's own downstream tests cover LLM-as-judge evaluation and hiring.

**Multi-agent verification with aspect verifiers (Lifshitz et al., ICLR 2025 workshop)**

- **What aspect verifiers are:** They are off-the-shelf LLMs prompted to verify specific aspects of candidate outputs through binary True/False approvals.
- **How they're combined:** Their binary outputs can be easily combined across multiple models through simple voting mechanisms.
- **Reported results:** The BoN-MAV algorithm demonstrates stronger scaling patterns than self-consistency and reward model verification, and the authors test self-improvement, where the same base model is used to both generate and verify outputs.

**Connecting the two**

The verification paper's abstract doesn't measure whether its verifiers fail together. The correlated-errors paper suggests that verifiers built on same-family or same-architecture models, including the self-improvement setup, could share blind spots and so add less independent checking than the vote count suggests. A separate preprint, which I found only as a summary, models verifier cascades with correlated verifiers and finds that cascade gains diminish with each additional gate. Its own result is not confirmed here, so check the original paper before relying on it.

A related ICLR 2026 submission reports that correlation-aware routing that pairs generators with low-correlation verifiers helps, citing ρ = 0.54 for cross-family pairs. The snippet cut off before the comparison figure, so I can't report the full result.

**Retry limits**

- **Per-request budget:** "If a request has already failed three times, we let the failure bubble up to the caller." The article says a fourth attempt is unlikely to help because the whole datacenter is probably overloaded.
- **Per-client budget:** Clients track the share of their requests that are retries. "A request will only be retried as long as this ratio is below 10%."
- **Effect on load:** Without the client budget, worst-case load approaches 3X, which the article calls significant. With it, "layering on the per-client retry budget (a 10% retry ratio) reduces the growth to just 1.1x in the general case."

**Adaptive throttling**

Each client tracks `requests` and `accepts` over the last two minutes. "Clients can continue to issue requests to the backend until `requests` is K times as large as `accepts`." After that, requests are rejected locally with a calculated probability. The article prefers K = 2. Lower values throttle more aggressively, and higher values less so. The probability formula appears only as an image, so its exact form isn't in the text.

**Criticality**

- Four values exist: `CRITICAL_PLUS`, `CRITICAL`, `SHEDDABLE_PLUS`, and `SHEDDABLE`.
- Under quota exhaustion, "will only reject requests of a given criticality if it's already rejecting all requests of all lower criticalities."
- "When a task is itself overloaded, it will reject requests of lower criticalities sooner."
- Criticality propagates to downstream calls by default, and it is typically set at the HTTP frontends.

**"Overloaded; don't retry" errors**

Backends return this error when their histograms of attempt counts show many retries, which suggests other tasks are also overloaded. It replaces the standard "task overloaded" error, which triggers retries. Where a whole layer is overloaded, "requests should not be retried and errors should bubble up all the way to the caller." In deep dependency stacks, a failed request "should only be retried by Backend B, the layer immediately above it," which avoids a combinatorial retry explosion.

**Deadlines**

The article does not discuss deadlines, so I have no recommendations to extract on that topic.

I didn't find a controlled study that compares temperature 0 and 0.7 on WebArena or BrowserGym web navigation. The closest evidence comes from a tool-calling preprint, plus several sources on run-to-run variance and benchmark reproducibility.

**Tool calling at different temperatures:** A recent preprint on tool-calling accuracy found that greedy decoding with zero temperature fails to fully activate the model's internal knowledge required for correct tool usage, and that parallel sampling substantially improved performance. The authors also state that increasing the sampling temperature not only elicits relevant knowledge more effectively but also increases the frequency with which such knowledge appears. This is a preprint, and its setup is not web navigation, so treat it as suggestive rather than settled.

**Variance in web agent runs:** A web-agent study reports that even at a fixed temperature, LLM outputs vary across runs due to hardware-level non-determinism in distributed inference. It adds that a given task may succeed in one run and fail in another for reasons unrelated to agent capability. It also notes that BrowserGym and Playwright can encounter timeouts, slow page loads, or intermittent server errors. This matters for your comparison: a difference between temperature 0 and 0.7 could be swamped by run-to-run noise unless you repeat runs.

**Environment fragility in BrowserGym/AgentLab:** One paper using BrowserGym and AgentLab notes that the original BrowserGym evaluation framework reports significant error rates across benchmarks due to browser crashes, network timeouts, and environment state corruption. To mitigate this, it retried each task up to 10 times on failure, fully reset the WebArena instance between evaluation runs, and used isolated browser contexts per task, and a residual error rate still remained.

**Reproducibility tooling:** The BrowserGym ecosystem paper describes a Study class that contains a dictionary of information about reproducibility, including benchmark version, package version, commit hash, os version, and time stamp. That lets you isolate package and system effects from the temperature effect you're testing.

**WebArena reliability issues:** WebArena Verified audits all 812 tasks, repairs misaligned evaluations and clarifies ambiguous instructions, and provides improved results reporting with template-level macro averages, 95% confidence intervals, and failure-mode breakdowns. Using the verified version and its confidence intervals would make a temperature comparison more trustworthy than the original WebArena scores.

**General guidance (weaker evidence):** Vendor and blog sources recommend low temperature for tool calls. One says that for reliable agents the rule is: deterministic tool calls and JSON/structured outputs with temperature 0 to 0.2. These are practitioner heuristics, not benchmark results, and one of them also notes that full determinism is rarely guaranteed in practice even at temperature 0.

**Practical takeaway:** If you run this comparison yourself, use the WebArena Verified tasks, run each temperature across several seeds or repeats, and report confidence intervals. Pin the model version and log the BrowserGym/AgentLab versions. Then a 0 vs 0.7 difference can be separated from noise.

**Title:** When Agents Disagree With Themselves: Behavioral Consistency as an Uncertainty Signal for LLM Agents

**Author:** Aman Mehta (Snowflake AI Research). Accepted to the ICML 2026 Workshop on Statistical Frameworks for Uncertainty in Agentic Systems.

**Action sequences per 10 runs**
- Repeated runs of the same agent on identical inputs produced 2.3–4.2 distinct action sequences per 10 runs, depending on the model.
- Per model: Claude Sonnet 4.5 2.3, GPT-5 2.4, Gemini 3 Pro 3.2, Llama 3.1 70B 4.2.

**Consistency and accuracy (HotpotQA, 200 questions)**
- Consistent tasks (≤2 unique sequences) reached 82–87% accuracy; inconsistent tasks (≥4) reached 41–65%.
- Gaps by model: Gemini 86.5% vs. 41.2%, GPT-5 85.9% vs. 53.1%, Claude 86.4% vs. 60.3%, Llama 82.3% vs. 64.7%.
- The paper reports the gap survives Holm-Bonferroni correction, but the stratified analysis shows it is weaker or absent in some difficulty strata.

**Divergence timing**
- Pooled, 18.8% of tasks diverged by step 2.
- Llama diverged by step 2 in 50.5% of tasks, versus 4–6% for Claude and GPT-5.
- Llama's early-diverging tasks had 71.7% accuracy, versus 85.8% for late-diverging tasks.
- Step-2 agreement alone was near chance for predicting failure (AUROC 0.49–0.60).

**Failure detection**
- Consistency metrics reached AUROC 0.62–0.78 across models.
- On a 100-question split, behavioral consistency beat verbalized confidence for all three models tested (e.g., Llama 0.739 vs. 0.481).

**Selective prediction and voting**
- Answering only when all 3 runs agree gave 87–88% accuracy at 54–62% coverage for Llama, Claude, and GPT-5, a 6–14pp gain over single-run baselines. Gemini gained only about 1pp.
- Majority voting over k=3 gained only 0–2pp.

**Benchmarks**
- SWE-bench Verified (50 tasks, 5 repositories, 1,000 runs) preserved the consistency ranking: Claude < GPT-5 < Gemini < Llama by coefficient of variation.
- Mean trajectory length varied about 7.8× across models (GPT-5 10.5 steps to Gemini 81.8).
- Single-run evaluations produced a model ranking that differed from the multi-run ranking 29.3% of the time.

**Temperature effect**
- A small ablation (20 questions, 5 runs) found unique sequences generally rose with temperature.
- Claude and Gemini were near-deterministic at T=0.0 (1.0 sequences), but Llama stayed at 2.3 and GPT-5 still diverged, so temperature alone does not explain inconsistency.
- Llama's values in the appendix table are not monotonic (2.3, 2.1, 3.3), which the text does not address.

**Recommendations**
- The paper recommends multi-run evaluation for agent benchmarks, consistency-based selective prediction, and runtime consistency monitoring.
- It suggests better first-query formulation could reduce downstream variance, since divergence concentrates at step 2.
- It does not recommend early divergence as a rerun trigger or confidence proxy. It reports that step-2 agreement is weak for failure prediction, and that answer-level consistency is the stronger signal.

**Limitations noted by the author:** the study is exploratory with uncorrected raw p-values, the Hard-stratum annotation was done by one annotator, and causality cannot be established from observational data.
