# Reliability engineering and variance reduction for deadline-bound LLM agent systems (as of October 2026)

Reading notes for the writer:
- "Task brief" means the numbers supplied with the assignment (scores 100, 100, 100, 44.9, 38.2, 15, 10; p50 3 s, p95 9 s; 32 concurrent calls; 120-150 s client wait; 200-260 calls in a good run; 139 calls and 9 unanswered calls in one bad run).
- "Own estimate" marks numbers I computed myself (a lognormal fit to p50 = 3 s / p95 = 9 s, a Monte Carlo simulation of one agent loop, exact binomial calculations). They are not from a source.
- "Background" marks classic systems sources. "Search summary only" marks papers whose numbers I took from a search-result summary without reading the full text; treat those as leads to verify.

## 1. Tail latency: what do hedged requests, tied requests, adaptive timeouts and retry budgets recommend, and what timeout and hedge delay fit a call with p50 = 3 s and p95 = 9 s?

### Takeaway
The measured failure (9 calls unanswered for 120-150 s) is a hang problem, and the fix with by far the largest effect is a short per-attempt cap (about 20 s) plus one backup request after roughly the p90-p95 of observed latency (7-9 s), with the loser cancelled. By my simulation this brings one agent's model-wait time at a 6 % hang rate from about 780 s back to about 270 s, for 10-16 % extra calls.

### Cited Findings
- Background. Fan-out amplifies rare slowness: if one server is slow 1 time in 100, a request that touches 100 servers is slow 63 % of the time. — [The Tail at Scale, summary by The Morning Paper](https://blog.acolyer.org/2015/01/15/the-tail-at-scale/)
- Background. Hedged request: send the same request again only after the first has been outstanding longer than the 95th-percentile expected latency "for this class of requests", then use whichever answers first; this limits extra load to about 5 %. — [Dean and Barroso 2013, CACM](https://cacm.acm.org/research/the-tail-at-scale/); [summary](https://blog.acolyer.org/2015/01/15/the-tail-at-scale/)
- Background. Google's BigTable benchmark (1,000 keys over 100 servers): a hedge after 10 ms cut the 99.9th-percentile latency from 1,800 ms to 74 ms with 2 % more requests. Quoted from memory of the paper; the CACM page returned HTTP 403 in this session, so verify before printing. — [Dean and Barroso 2013, CACM](https://cacm.acm.org/research/the-tail-at-scale/)
- Background. Tied requests: enqueue on two servers at once and let each cancel the other when one starts work; in a real Google system the median fell 16 % and the 99.9th percentile fell 40 %. This needs server-side cross-cancellation. — [summary](https://blog.acolyer.org/2015/01/15/the-tail-at-scale/)
- Background. Other techniques in the same paper: "good enough" results (return once enough of the fan-out has answered), canary requests (send to one or two servers first to catch a request or backend that stalls), and latency-induced probation (stop sending to a slow machine, keep probing it, readmit it when it recovers). — [summary](https://blog.acolyer.org/2015/01/15/the-tail-at-scale/)
- Background. Google SRE retry rules: a request is attempted at most three times; a client only retries while its retries are under 10 % of its requests. Without the per-client budget worst-case load grows about 3x, with it about 1.1x. Retries should happen at one layer only, to avoid a combinatorial retry explosion. — [Google SRE book, Handling Overload](https://sre.google/sre-book/handling-overload/)
- Background. Client-side adaptive throttling: track requests and accepts over two minutes, and start rejecting locally once requests exceed K times accepts (K = 2 preferred). Requests carry a criticality (CRITICAL_PLUS, CRITICAL, SHEDDABLE_PLUS, SHEDDABLE), and lower criticalities are shed first. — [Google SRE book, Handling Overload](https://sre.google/sre-book/handling-overload/)
- LLM-specific, 2026. A typical LLM call is described as p50 about 8 s and p95 about 18 s; "A retry policy designed for 50ms RPCs does not survive contact with an 8-second LLM call." The author recommends hedging when the primary exceeds its measured p90 (or p95 for cross-provider failover), a hedge budget capped at 5-10 % of base traffic, a global retry cap of 5-15 %, and separate budgets for timeouts versus errors. — [Tian Pan, May 2026](https://tianpan.co/blog/2026/05/02/tail-tolerant-retry-policy-llm-gateway-latency-cliff)
- Same source: with a 10 s per-attempt timeout, 1 s backoff and three sequential retries, a model p99 of 18 s turns into a caller-visible p99 of about 33 s; sequential failover across three providers can add 30 s. Hedging gives min(primary, hedge) where retrying gives primary + retry. The outcome claims in this post are the author's estimates, not measurements. — [Tian Pan, May 2026](https://tianpan.co/blog/2026/05/02/tail-tolerant-retry-policy-llm-gateway-latency-cliff)
- Adaptive hedging in a simulation of 50,000 requests with 5 % stragglers at 10x latency: hedging at the observed p90 (tracked with a quantile sketch over 30-60 s windows) cut p99 from 65.0 ms to 17.3 ms (about 74 %) for 8.9 % extra requests, with p50 unchanged. A static hedge at 10 ms gave 17.5 ms for 7.7 % overhead; a static hedge at 50 ms gave 54.9 ms for 2.1 %. The library was not in production; these are simulation numbers. — [InfoQ, adaptive hedged requests](https://www.infoq.com/articles/adaptive-hedged-requests-p99-latency/)
- Same source, on LLM inference: streaming endpoints return HTTP headers in 1-2 ms, so the hedge timer must run on time to first token, not on time to first byte. Calibrated on first byte the hedger fired on almost every call (about 100 % overhead); calibrated on first token the overhead was 17-19.8 %. — [InfoQ](https://www.infoq.com/articles/adaptive-hedged-requests-p99-latency/)
- Same source, when not to hedge: non-idempotent requests; a single-instance backend (the hedge lands on the same slow machine); CPU-saturated backends; services under about 1 request per second (too little data for the sketch); and services behind a shared rate limit, where a 20 % hedge rate could itself trigger throttling. — [InfoQ](https://www.infoq.com/articles/adaptive-hedged-requests-p99-latency/)
- A hedge budget of 10 % as a token bucket empties in about one second during a full outage, so hedging stops before it doubles backend load. — [InfoQ](https://www.infoq.com/articles/adaptive-hedged-requests-p99-latency/)
- An open-source hedging library aimed at LLM inference claims a 75-96 % p99 reduction for 5-10 % cost overhead and offers fixed, percentile, adaptive and "workload-aware" (prompt length, model complexity) delay strategies with `max_hedges: 1` and loser cancellation. README claim, not independently verified. — [crucible_hedging README](https://github.com/North-Shore-AI/crucible_hedging)
- Cost framing: hedging at p95 means "paying twice for 5% of requests". — [dev.to, Request Hedging](https://dev.to/gabrielanhaia/request-hedging-the-tail-at-scale-technique-most-teams-skip-2j37)
- The OpenAI Python client waits 10 minutes by default and retries twice by default, so a wrapper that owns timeouts and retries should set `timeout=` and `max_retries=0` explicitly. Cited from memory of the README, not re-fetched in this session. — [openai-python README](https://github.com/openai/openai-python)

### Inferences
- Own estimate. A lognormal distribution through p50 = 3 s and p95 = 9 s has p75 = 4.7 s, p90 = 7.1 s, p99 = 14.2 s and p99.9 = 23.6 s. Under it, P(latency > 12 s) = 1.9 %, P(> 20 s) = 0.23 %, P(> 30 s) = 0.03 %. A healthy call essentially never needs more than 25-30 s, so a wait of 120-150 s buys nothing: a call that has not answered by about 20 s is hung, not slow.
- Own estimate. The latency is therefore a mixture: a normal body plus a "no reply" mass. In the bad run it was 9 of about 148 attempts, roughly 6 %. With 260 calls per run, even a 1 % hang rate gives a 93 % chance of at least one hang per run (1 - 0.99^260), and each hang costs one agent 120-150 s, which is 30-40 normal calls. This is the same arithmetic as the 63 % fan-out example.
- Own estimate, Monte Carlo of one agent loop of 65 sequential calls (seconds of model wait: median / p95; extra calls):

| Policy | hang 0 % | hang 1 % | hang 3 % | hang 6 % | extra calls at 6 % |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| wait 135 s, then retry (today) | 242 / 283 | 283 / 531 | 504 / 898 | 782 / 1317 | +6 % |
| cap 30 s, then retry | 243 / 283 | 260 / 324 | 299 / 390 | 363 / 481 | +6 % |
| cap 20 s, then retry | 242 / 282 | 254 / 305 | 282 / 350 | 325 / 413 | +7 % |
| cap 12 s, then retry | 243 / 283 | 250 / 295 | 267 / 317 | 292 / 354 | +8 % (kills 2 % of healthy calls) |
| hedge at 9 s, round cap 25 s | 239 / 275 | 245 / 280 | 256 / 300 | 277 / 328 | +11 % |
| hedge at 7 s, round cap 20 s | 235 / 267 | 240 / 274 | 250 / 289 | 266 / 312 | +16 % |
| hedge at 5 s, round cap 20 s | 228 / 257 | 232 / 262 | 239 / 273 | 252 / 292 | +27 % |

- Reading of the table: almost all of the gain comes from shortening the cap (782 s to 325 s at a 6 % hang rate). Hedging adds a further 15-20 % and, unlike a very short cap, does not throw away a primary that is slow but alive. Moving the hedge from 9 s to 5 s buys little and more than doubles the overhead.
- Recommended starting values for this system (own estimate): connect timeout 5 s; hedge after 8 s, then adaptive at the rolling p90 of the last 50-60 completions of that call type, clamped to 5-12 s; per-round cap 20 s for agent steps and 25-30 s for long-output extraction calls; at most one backup; at most three rounds; SDK retries off. If streaming works through the proxy, trigger the hedge on "no first token after 6-8 s", which separates a hung call from a long answer.
- Timeouts tuned to output length: completion time is roughly time-to-first-token plus output tokens divided by tokens per second, so set the cap per call type from logged data (cap = p99 of first-token time + max_tokens / slow-case token rate) and set `max_tokens` on every call so the bound is real. I found no source giving a formula; this is a reasoned rule.
- Cost under the cap of 32: a hedge occupies one extra slot for at most the remainder of the round (about 12 s). With four agent loops plus a page-extraction fan-out, a hedge budget of 10-15 % of calls and at most 4 slots for hedges keeps the system below 32. More important, a short cap frees slots: under today's policy 9 hung calls each held a slot for 2 minutes.
- Hedging does not help if hangs come from the team's own traffic exceeding the 32-call limit (requests queued at the proxy). Then extra requests make it worse, as the "shared rate limit" warning says. A client-side semaphore below 32 rules that cause out; no second run of the team should be active during the final evaluation because the limit is shared across runs.
- The hung calls in the bad run looked independent per request (9 of about 148 failed while the rest of the run continued), which is the case hedging handles. If the whole proxy degrades, hedging to the same proxy cannot help; a fallback route to another model through the metered proxy can.
- Canary requests map directly onto "the very first call got no reply": send 2-3 one-token calls in parallel at start-up and use the first that returns as both warm-up and health probe.

### Gaps
- No published latency distribution for Qwen3.8-Flash-Next through this proxy; all percentiles beyond p50 and p95 are from my lognormal fit. Whether the proxy supports streaming, and the first-token distribution, are unknown.
- Unknown whether cancelling a request client-side makes the proxy stop generation and release the concurrency slot. If it does not, cancelled losers still count against the 32 for a while. This can be tested in ten minutes by cancelling 20 calls and watching whether 32 fresh ones are admitted.
- I found no measured, peer-reviewed study of hedging LLM API calls; the LLM-specific sources are engineering posts and one simulation.
- Whether the 9 unanswered calls were proxy-side hangs, queueing behind the team's own concurrency, or dropped connections is not known; it decides how much hedging helps versus a plain short cap.

## 2. Variance and reliability measurement: pass^k, "AI Agents That Matter", HAL, temperature-0 variance studies; how many runs separate 80 % from 95 %, and what cheap proxies exist?

### Takeaway
Agent systems that succeed most of the time still fail on a large share of repeated trials, and full runs are far too expensive to measure this: about 30 full runs are needed to tell 80 % from 95 % reliability, so the team has to measure per call and per stage, on saved pages and with injected faults.

### Cited Findings
- tau-bench introduced pass^k, the probability that all k independent trials of the same task succeed. Function-calling agents such as gpt-4o succeeded on under 50 % of tasks and were inconsistent: pass^8 under 25 % in the retail domain. — [Yao et al. 2024, tau-bench](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.12045)
- pass^k differs from pass@k (at least one of k succeeds); Anthropic's model cards adopted pass^k after tau-bench. — [Sierra blog](https://sierra.ai/blog/tau-bench-shaping-development-evaluation-agents)
- Leaderboard snapshot seen in search results (not opened in full): on tau2-bench the top pass^1 values are 85-88 %; on the newer tau3 banking knowledge track the top entry, Qwen 3.8 Max, is at 55.2 % pass^1. — [taubench.com](https://taubench.com/)
- "AI Agents That Matter": because models are stochastic, simply calling a model repeatedly raises accuracy, and such simple retry baselines beat complex agent architectures on HumanEval at much lower cost; the authors ran each agent five times and reported means; they found pervasive reproducibility shortcomings in WebArena and HumanEval evaluations that inflate accuracy. — [Kapoor et al., project page](https://agents.cs.princeton.edu/); [arXiv 2407.01502](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.01502)
- HAL (Holistic Agent Leaderboard): 21,730 agent rollouts across 9 models and 9 benchmarks for about $40,000; higher reasoning effort reduced accuracy in the majority of runs; log inspection found agents taking shortcuts such as searching for the benchmark instead of solving the task. — [Kapoor et al., HAL, arXiv 2510.11977](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2510.11977); [HAL site](https://hal.cs.princeton.edu/about)
- Same agent, identical inputs, 10 runs: 2.3 (Claude Sonnet 4.5), 2.4 (GPT-5), 3.2 (Gemini 3 Pro) and 4.2 (Llama 3.1 70B) distinct action sequences. Tasks with consistent behaviour (at most 2 distinct sequences) reached 82-87 % accuracy; inconsistent ones (4 or more) 41-65 %. Single-run rankings of models differed from multi-run rankings 29.3 % of the time on a SWE-bench Verified subset. Exploratory workshop paper by one author. — [Mehta 2026, arXiv 2602.11619](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.11619)
- Same paper: behavioural consistency predicted failure with AUROC 0.62-0.78 and beat verbalised confidence (for example 0.739 versus 0.481 for Llama). Agreement at step 2 alone was near chance (AUROC 0.49-0.60). — [Mehta 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.11619)
- Search summary only. Across 60,000 SWE-bench Verified trajectories, single-run pass@1 varied by 2.2-6.0 percentage points; the standard deviation stayed above 1.5 points at temperature 0; trajectories diverged within the first few percent of generated tokens and the divergence compounded. — [Engineering Reliable Coding Agents, arXiv 2608.13867](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2608.13867)
- Search summary only. Five repeats of one configuration: of 32 scenario points, 15 passed all five times, 1 failed all five, and 16 were flaky, so variance sat in a subset of unstable tasks. — [AgentLens, arXiv 2607.06624](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2607.06624)
- Search summary only. ReliabilityBench proposes measuring consistency under repeated execution together with robustness to perturbations and tolerance of injected faults. — [ReliabilityBench, arXiv 2601.06112](https://arxiv.org/html/2601.06112v1)
- Web-agent harnesses add their own noise: BrowserGym and Playwright runs hit timeouts, slow page loads and intermittent server errors; one group retried each task up to 10 times and reset the site between runs and still had residual errors. Search summary only; I could not tell which of the two papers made which statement. — [arXiv 2606.15017](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2606.15017); [arXiv 2604.07776](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2604.07776)
- WebArena Verified audited all 812 tasks, repaired misaligned checks and reports 95 % confidence intervals and failure-mode breakdowns. — [WebArena Verified, NeurIPS 2025](https://neurips.cc/virtual/2025/124576)
- A statistical treatment of evaluations (standard errors, clustered questions, paired comparisons, power analysis). Cited from memory, not re-fetched. — [Miller 2024, Adding Error Bars to Evals](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.00640)

### Inferences
- Own estimate. The team's record is 3 runs at 100 out of 7; a 95 % Wilson interval for the underlying rate of a top-score run is 16 % to 75 %. The scores are bimodal (three at 100, four at 10-45), which points to run-level failures of the time budget, not to gradual quality loss.
- Own estimate, exact binomial. To reject "reliability is at most 80 %" at the 5 % level with 80 % power when the truth is 95 %: 30 runs, of which at least 28 must pass. Comparing two versions (80 % versus 95 %) head to head needs about 57 runs per version one-sided, 72 two-sided. At 20 minutes per run and a shared concurrency limit this is 10 hours or more, so it is not available.
- Own estimate. What small samples can say: 10 passes out of 10 still happens 10.7 % of the time for an 80 % system (0.8^10), so it does not exclude 80 %; the Wilson interval for 10/10 is 72-100 %. Fourteen straight passes are needed to exclude 80 % (0.8^14 = 4.4 %), and a truly 95 % system produces 14 straight passes only 49 % of the time. Certifying 95 % with zero failures needs 59 straight passes (0.95^59 = 4.8 %). For "best of three" in the final: a 3-in-7 system gets at least one good run with probability about 81 %; an 80 % system 99 %.
- Cheap proxies that give hundreds of samples per hour instead of three:
  1. Per-call statistics. Every run has 200-260 calls, so three runs give 600+ samples of latency and of the no-reply rate (standard error under 1 point at a 3 % rate).
  2. Per-stage success on replayed pages. Save every page an agent files during good runs; re-run extraction and the deterministic bid on the saved set 20 times. This measures extraction consistency without the websites and costs pages x 20 calls.
  3. Time margins as continuous metrics: seconds of slack at the investigation cut-off, time of the last new fact, time from "form started" to "signed". A margin shrinking from 300 s to 40 s is visible in one run; a pass rate is not.
  4. Fault injection. Wrap the client so that a chosen share of calls hang or run 3x slower, and require that the run still signs a full bid. This tests the mechanism on demand, where waiting for a bad proxy day does not.
  5. Behavioural consistency: number of distinct action sequences per site over a few runs, as in the Mehta study, marks the sites or subtasks where the agent is unstable.
- Report results as pass^k over the runs available plus the stage table, not a single best score; the literature above treats single-run numbers as unreliable.

### Gaps
- I did not find a 2025-2026 study that measures run-to-run variance for multi-agent web research with a wall-clock deadline; the closest evidence is from coding and question-answering agents.
- The three "search summary only" papers were not read in full; their numbers need checking before they are quoted.
- No source gives a validated mapping from per-stage success rates to whole-run reliability; multiplying stage rates assumes independence, which a slow proxy violates (it hurts all stages at once).

## 3. Deadline-aware control: anytime behaviour, step budgets, budget-aware prompts, early stopping, and how to split and adapt investigation versus submission time

### Takeaway
Showing the model its remaining budget after every step measurably changes behaviour (same accuracy for about 31 % less cost in the main study), but the published effect is on stronger models and concerns mostly premature stopping, so for a hard deadline the budget must also be enforced in code, with the signature protected by a reserve computed from live latency.

### Cited Findings
- Budget-Aware Tool-Use (Google, November 2025): giving an agent a larger tool-call budget does not by itself help because standard agents lack budget awareness and hit a ceiling. ReAct with Gemini 2.5 Pro on BrowseComp scored 10.3, 10.5 and 12.6 at budgets of 10, 30 and 100, and at budget 100 used only 14.24 searches and 1.36 page visits on average. — [Liu et al. 2025, arXiv 2511.17006](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.17006v1)
- The Budget Tracker is a block appended after every tool result with used and remaining units per tool ("Query Budget Used: [number], Query Budget Remaining: [number], URL Budget Used: ..., URL Budget Remaining: ...") plus an initial policy with four tiers: HIGH (70 % or more remaining: 3-5 diverse queries, 2-3 URLs), MEDIUM (30-70 %: 2-3 refined queries, 1-2 URLs), LOW (10-30 %: 1 query, at most 1 URL), CRITICAL (under 10 %, or one budget at zero: avoid the depleted tool). — [Liu et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.17006v1)
- Effect at equal budget (100 per tool, mean of three runs): Gemini 2.5 Pro 12.6 to 14.6 on BrowseComp; Gemini 2.5 Flash 9.7 to 10.7; Claude Sonnet 4 12.2 to 14.0; similar gains of 1.3-2.6 points on the two other benchmarks. — [Liu et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.17006v1)
- Efficiency: the tracker at budget 10 matched ReAct at budget 100 (12.8 % versus 12.6 %) with 40.4 % fewer searches and 31.3 % lower cost. — [Liu et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.17006v1)
- The fuller framework (BATS) keeps a checklist of clues with status marks, verifies each constraint of a candidate answer (satisfied, contradicted, unverifiable) and then decides SUCCESS, CONTINUE (dig deeper) or PIVOT (switch direction while budget remains). After such a decision the raw trajectory is replaced by a summary of key steps, findings and failure causes; the trace is refreshed every 10 iterations. With early stopping the run ends at the first verified success. — [Liu et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.17006v1)
- BATS results at budget 100: 24.6 versus 12.6 on BrowseComp, 46.0 versus 31.5 on BrowseComp-ZH. Ablation with early stopping: full 18.7; without planning 17.0; without verification 15.4; without both 14.6. BATS passed 37 % on BrowseComp-ZH at about $0.23, where a parallel majority-vote baseline needed over $0.50 for a comparable result. — [Liu et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.17006v1)
- The paper attributes the ceiling of standard agents to stopping early, either because the agent believes it has the answer or because it gives up. — [Liu et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.17006v1)
- Background. An anytime algorithm can return a valid answer whenever it is interrupted, and the answer improves with more time. Not fetched in this session. — [Wikipedia, Anytime algorithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anytime_algorithm)
- Background. "Good enough" results: return once enough of a fan-out has answered instead of waiting for the slowest part. — [The Tail at Scale, summary](https://blog.acolyer.org/2015/01/15/the-tail-at-scale/)
- Task brief: a signed partial bid scores its filled positions and an unsigned bid scores nothing; ranking is eligibility, then quality, then lower cost x time; form and signature take about 4 minutes; the investigation is cut 8 minutes before the end.

### Inferences
- The scoring rule makes the signature the one step that must never be late, and makes investigation time worth less with every minute. This is the textbook case for an anytime design: hold a valid, submittable bid from as early as possible and improve it until a hard "start submitting" time.
- The fixed 8-minute reserve is twice the usual 4 minutes, which is reasonable while one hung call can cost 150 s. Once calls are capped at about 20 s, the reserve can be computed during the run: reserve = browser-only time of the submission stage + (number of model calls in that stage) x (p90 latency seen in this run) x 1.5, with a floor of about 5.5 minutes (own estimate). On a slow-proxy day this grows by itself; on a normal day it returns up to 2 minutes to the investigation.
- Because an unsigned bid scores zero and the final is a single run, I would not lower the floor below the slowest submission seen in tests plus 60-90 s. The cheaper gain is on the other side: stop the investigation as soon as every required record is present and checked, which also improves the time tie-breaker.
- Budget prompts have two different jobs here. In the paper they mainly stop agents from quitting early. This system's failure is the opposite (an agent that loops until the deadline), and the LOW and CRITICAL tiers address that only if the model obeys. The paper tested Gemini 2.5 and Claude Sonnet 4; a small fast model may follow the block less well, so a code-side step budget, a stall detector and a forced stop are needed as well.
- Step budgets per subgoal: give each site agent a list of record types it must produce and a step allowance per item; when an item's allowance is used up the supervisor marks it "unresolved" and makes the agent move on (the PIVOT decision), so one hard item cannot eat the whole window.
- Saving partial results early: file every extracted record to a store outside the agent's context the moment it is found, and recompute the bid whenever the store changes. Then the cut-off, a restart or a crash never loses work, and the bid at any time is the best available.
- If the form can be opened and partly filled while agents are still working, the 4-minute submission stage overlaps with the investigation and only the final update and the signature remain sequential. Whether the form tolerates this is a property of the challenge site.

### Gaps
- No study of budget-aware prompting on Qwen-family flash models, and none with a wall-clock (seconds) budget; the evidence is for counted tool calls.
- I found no agent-specific paper on choosing the split between a work phase and a commit phase under a deadline; the reserve formula above is my own.
- Whether the bid form allows early partial filling, later edits, or re-signing is unknown from the brief.

## 4. Redundancy at decision points: self-consistency, voting, verifiers, dual extraction, racing a second agent; when does it help and when are errors correlated?

### Takeaway
Redundancy pays where the copies fail independently and the decision is checkable (extraction of bid-relevant values, the "am I done" decision, the signature path); it pays little as blanket voting on every agent step, because repeated samples of one model share most of their errors.

### Cited Findings
- Self-consistency: sample several reasoning paths and take the majority answer; the original source of the voting idea. Background, cited from memory and not re-fetched. — [Wang et al. 2022, arXiv 2203.11171](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.11171)
- More calls are not always better: with majority voting, performance can first rise and then fall as the number of model calls grows, because extra calls help on "easy" queries and hurt on "hard" ones; the best number of calls can be estimated from a small sample. — [Chen et al., NeurIPS 2024, arXiv 2403.02419](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.02419)
- Errors are correlated across models: on one leaderboard dataset, two models that are both wrong pick the same wrong answer about 60 % of the time; correlation is higher for more accurate models and for models from the same developer or base architecture. — [Kim et al., ICML 2025](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v267/kim25e.html); [arXiv 2506.07962](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.07962)
- Agent-level voting gains are small: majority voting over 3 runs gained 0-2 points, while answering only when all 3 runs agree gave 87-88 % accuracy at 54-62 % coverage, a 6-14 point gain over a single run (about 1 point for Gemini). Agreement is more useful as a signal of doubt than as a vote. — [Mehta 2026, arXiv 2602.11619](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.11619)
- Retries are not independent: an independent-attempts model overestimated pass@3 on SWE-bench Verified by 17.4 points (98.6 % predicted versus 81.2 % observed). Abstract only; single-author preprint. — [Yang 2026, arXiv 2605.08563](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.08563)
- Multi-agent verification: several off-the-shelf models each check one aspect of a candidate with a True/False verdict, and the verdicts are combined by voting; the authors report better scaling than self-consistency and than reward-model verification, also when the same base model generates and verifies. — [Lifshitz et al. 2025, arXiv 2502.20379](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.20379)
- A verification step that checks each constraint of a proposed answer was worth 3.3 points in the BATS ablation (18.7 with, 15.4 without), and BATS reached the same accuracy as a parallel majority-vote baseline at less than half the cost. — [Liu et al. 2025, arXiv 2511.17006](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.17006v1)
- Simple repetition baselines can beat complex agents at lower cost, so redundancy should be compared against "just call it again". — [Kapoor et al., AI Agents That Matter](https://agents.cs.princeton.edu/)
- Search summary only. A reviewer-gated loop that samples candidates one after another and stops at the first one the reviewer approves outperformed verifier and critic variants at every budget while using far fewer samples; evaluated with Qwen-family agents and a trained reviewer. — [SWE-Review, arXiv 2607.06065](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2607.06065)

### Inferences
- Independence is the test. Two samples of the same model on the same page text share the model, the prompt and the input, so they share most errors. Three ways to de-correlate, cheapest first: deterministic checks (types, ranges, units, totals, cross-record consistency), which share nothing with the model; a different view of the input (table-structured text versus raw text, or a different chunk order); a different model for the second opinion (the cheap decision model for yes/no questions, a frontier model as tie-breaker).
- Dual extraction with comparison fits this system well. Extraction is one call per page, it runs in parallel, and only pages that feed the bid matter. Run a second extraction with a varied prompt view on those pages, compare field by field in code, and send only disagreeing fields to a third opinion. Own estimate of cost: one extra call per bid-relevant page (perhaps 15-40 calls on a 200-260 call run), near zero added wall time when run in parallel under the cap.
- The "am I done" decision is the second good place: BATS shows un-checked agents stop too early. A code-side checklist of required record types, plus a cheap yes-probability from the decision model on "does this page contain X" before filing or discarding a document, covers it for a few short calls.
- Racing a second agent from a different start is a portfolio strategy: it helps when run times are heavy-tailed and failures depend on the starting path (see question 5). Under a cap of 32 it should use capacity that is free anyway: when one site agent finishes early, start a second agent on the site that is furthest behind, entering by search where the first entered by navigation, and let both write to the same record store.
- Voting on every navigation step triples the call count for a 0-2 point gain and is not worth it under a call cap. Disagreement between two cheap proposals can instead be used as a trigger to spend more (a verifier call) at forks that matter.
- The signature path is a different kind of redundancy: the action must happen once, so the calls leading to it can be sent in duplicate from the start (hedge delay zero), but the side effect (requesting the one-time code, submitting) must stay single and idempotent in code.

### Gaps
- No source measures dual extraction with comparison on web pages for typed records; the benefit estimate rests on the general correlation results.
- The 60 % same-wrong-answer figure is from one multiple-choice dataset; correlation for free-form extraction is unknown.
- Whether the cheap decision model's errors are independent of Qwen's on this content is unknown and can only be measured on saved pages.

## 5. Restart and recovery: checkpoint and restart with a summary, supervisor timeouts, "restart beats continue", and preserving what was learned

### Takeaway
A stalled or looping agent should be stopped by a supervisor and restarted with a fresh context that contains only a code-built summary of facts found, pages visited and dead ends; the evidence says a failed attempt left in the context makes the next one worse, and restart theory says cut-offs help exactly when run times are heavy-tailed, as they are here.

### Cited Findings
- Background. For algorithms with heavy-tailed run times, restarting improves expected run time; with a known distribution a fixed cut-off is optimal, and without that knowledge Luby's universal schedule is within a logarithmic factor of optimal (Luby, Sinclair and Zuckerman 1993). — [Runtime Distributions and Criteria for Restarts, arXiv 1709.10405](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1709.10405)
- Context contamination: when a failed attempt stays in the context window, later attempts run at a higher per-step error rate. Fitted to SWE-bench Verified, the error-rate ratio after a failure was 7.1, and a model that assumes independent retries overestimated pass@3 by 17.4 points (98.6 % versus 81.2 %). The paper proves that clearing the context before a retry reduces the attempts needed, and derives an optimal attempt length for a fixed total budget. Abstract only; single-author preprint, not peer reviewed as far as I could see. — [Yang 2026, Why Retrying Fails, arXiv 2605.08563](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.08563)
- BATS replaces the raw trajectory with a summary of key steps, findings and failure causes whenever it continues or pivots, and refreshes the trace every 10 iterations, keeping a checklist whose entries are never deleted. — [Liu et al. 2025, arXiv 2511.17006](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.17006v1)
- Search summary only. A Luby-style campaign of 15 fresh sub-runs with conversation reset, in LLM-driven heuristic search for process control, reached a higher median (35.1 versus 33.5) but a lower best score (51.6 versus 55.5) than 52 ad-hoc independent runs, in about 4.1 hours instead of about 36. — [arXiv 2603.20537](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2603.20537)
- Search summary only. Sequential resampling gated by a reviewer (stop at the first approved candidate, at most K attempts) beat verifier and critic variants while using fewer samples. — [SWE-Review, arXiv 2607.06065](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2607.06065)
- Tree-search agents with backtracking exist for software tasks (Monte Carlo tree search with iterative refinement); I did not extract numbers. — [SWE-Search, arXiv 2410.20285](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.20285)
- Trajectories of the same agent diverge early and the divergence compounds (search summary only), and in one study 18.8 % of tasks had diverged by step 2. — [arXiv 2608.13867](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2608.13867); [Mehta 2026, arXiv 2602.11619](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.11619)
- Background. Latency-induced probation: take a slow component out of service and readmit it when it recovers. — [The Tail at Scale, summary](https://blog.acolyer.org/2015/01/15/the-tail-at-scale/)

### Inferences
- The observed failure "one agent looped until the deadline" is a heavy tail in time-to-completion: most runs finish a site in 5-8 minutes and a few never do. That is the condition under which a cut-off plus restart lowers expected time. With one known good-run duration, a fixed cut-off is the right form: restart an agent that has produced no new record or filed page for about 60-90 s, or that repeats the same action three times (own estimate of the thresholds; a normal step takes 3-9 s, so 75 s is 8-20 steps of nothing).
- Restart with a clean context and a summary built by code, not with the old transcript. The summary holds: records already filed, URLs visited, searches tried, and what led nowhere. This follows both the contamination result and the BATS design, and it keeps the rule that the model chooses the navigation.
- Vary the restart: a different entry point (site search versus menu navigation), a slightly higher temperature, or a reworded goal. A restart that replays the same start with the same prompt at low temperature tends to re-enter the same loop.
- Preserve learning outside the agent: the record store and the visited-URL set live in the orchestrator and are written at every step, so a restart, the cut-off, or a process crash loses nothing. Writing the store to disk after each stage also allows the submission stage to be retried without re-investigating.
- Limit restarts to two per site and stop restarting once the investigation window has under about 60 s left; a restart costs roughly 5-15 calls of re-orientation (own estimate).
- A restart is also the cheapest answer to an agent whose context has grown long: fewer input tokens per call means lower latency per step.

### Gaps
- I found no controlled experiment comparing "continue" with "restart with summary" for web navigation agents; the direct evidence is from coding agents, a theoretical model and one industrial search study.
- No published guidance on stall thresholds for web agents; the 60-90 s and three-repeat values are my estimates and should be set from logs of good runs (longest gap between two filed pages in a run that scored 100).
- The contamination paper was read as an abstract only.

## 6. Determinism: temperature, seeds, prompt caching and ordering; does a lower temperature reduce harmful variance for navigation?

### Takeaway
Temperature 0 and a fixed seed reduce variance but do not make hosted models deterministic, and no study shows that lowering temperature fixes navigation failures; use low temperature for extraction and form filling, accept variance in navigation, and control it with budgets, verification and restarts.

### Cited Findings
- Five models, eight tasks, ten runs per condition at temperature 0, top-p 1 and a fixed seed: accuracy varied by up to 15 % across runs, and the gap between best-possible and worst-possible accuracy reached 70 % (72 points for Mixtral on college math in the table). Raw-string agreement over 10 runs ranged from 0 % to 86 %; parsed-answer agreement from 12 % to 99.6 %. — [Atil et al. 2024, arXiv 2408.04667](https://arxiv.org/html/2408.04667v5)
- Same paper: longer outputs are less stable (output length correlates negatively with agreement); a locally run model without serving optimisations was deterministic, so the authors suspect continuous batching or prefix caching on hosted endpoints; they suggest limiting maximum generation tokens. — [Atil et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2408.04667v5)
- Agents: in a small ablation (20 questions, 5 runs) the number of distinct action sequences generally rose with temperature; Claude and Gemini were near-deterministic at temperature 0 (1.0 sequences) while Llama still produced 2.3 and GPT-5 still diverged, so temperature alone does not explain inconsistency. — [Mehta 2026, arXiv 2602.11619](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.11619)
- Search summary only. At temperature 0 the standard deviation of SWE-bench Verified pass@1 stayed above 1.5 points, attributed to infrastructure nondeterminism. — [arXiv 2608.13867](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2608.13867)
- Search summary only. A tool-calling study reports that greedy decoding at temperature 0 does not fully activate the knowledge needed for correct tool use and that parallel sampling at higher temperature improved results; not a web-navigation setting. — [arXiv 2606.10875](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2606.10875)
- A strong budget-aware search agent ran its acting model at temperature 0.7 and used temperature 0.0 only for answer selection and judging. — [Liu et al. 2025, arXiv 2511.17006](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.17006v1)
- Explanations given by practitioners: batched GPU arithmetic depends on what else is in the batch, requests are routed to different hardware, and mixture-of-experts routing can depend on batch context; none of this is controllable through API parameters. Blog-level sources. — [Towards AI, June 2026](https://pub.towardsai.net/the-mirage-of-determinism-at-temperature-zero-0f3992d0d0e1); [Label Studio](https://labelstud.io/learning-center/how-to-handle-non-determinism-in-agent-evaluation/)
- The BrowserGym ecosystem records benchmark version, package versions, commit hash and timestamps per study because results otherwise do not reproduce. — [BrowserGym ecosystem, arXiv 2412.05467](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.05467)

### Inferences
- Split the settings by call type. Extraction and form filling have one right answer: temperature 0 to 0.2, a seed if the proxy accepts one, structured output, a tight `max_tokens`. Navigation and search are exploration: keep the provider default or a moderate value, because determinism there mainly makes a bad path repeatable.
- Diversity is useful on purpose in two places: the second opinion in dual extraction, and a restarted or racing agent. Those calls should differ from the first (prompt view, entry point, slightly higher temperature).
- Keep the start of every prompt byte-identical across calls (system text, tool descriptions, fixed instructions first; changing content last). If the proxy caches prefixes this lowers latency; it also removes one source of run-to-run difference. Sort any lists that are fed to the model (links, records) so the order does not depend on arrival time of parallel tasks.
- The dominant variance in the team's runs is wall-clock (hangs, loops), not token-level. Even a perfectly deterministic model would have produced the bad runs, because the proxy's timing differs each time and timing changes which facts arrive before the cut-off.

### Gaps
- No controlled comparison of temperature settings for web navigation agents was found, and nothing on Qwen3.8-Flash-Next specifically (seed support, prompt caching through this proxy, default sampling settings).
- Ordering effects of parallel tool results on agent behaviour: I found no quantitative source; the advice to sort inputs is a precaution.

## 7. Which concrete measures can be added to the existing Python asyncio system in a few hours, with expected benefit and cost?

### Takeaway
Eight measures, ordered by expected benefit per hour of work: bounded and hedged model calls behind one concurrency governor, a start-up canary, a live deadline controller with an anytime bid, a stall-and-loop supervisor that restarts with a summary, redundancy only at extraction and at the "done" decision, and a measurement harness with fault injection. In a normal run they add roughly 15-25 % model calls and no wall time; in a bad run they are the difference between a full signed bid and a partial one.

### Cited Findings
- Hedge after the 95th percentile for about 5 % extra load; cancel the loser. — [Dean and Barroso 2013](https://cacm.acm.org/research/the-tail-at-scale/)
- At most three attempts per request and a retry budget of about 10 % of requests; retry at one layer only; shed low-criticality work first. — [Google SRE book](https://sre.google/sre-book/handling-overload/)
- For LLM calls, time the hedge on the first token, cap hedges at 5-10 % of traffic, and be careful behind a shared rate limit. — [InfoQ](https://www.infoq.com/articles/adaptive-hedged-requests-p99-latency/); [Tian Pan](https://tianpan.co/blog/2026/05/02/tail-tolerant-retry-policy-llm-gateway-latency-cliff)
- A per-step budget block with tiers changes agent behaviour; verification of each constraint and summary-based context refresh add further gains. — [Liu et al. 2025](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.17006v1)
- Clear the context before a retry. — [Yang 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.08563)
- Same-model repeats share errors; agreement is a better doubt signal than a vote. — [Kim et al. 2025](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v267/kim25e.html); [Mehta 2026](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.11619)
- Measure reliability over repeated trials (pass^k) and under injected faults. — [tau-bench](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.12045); [ReliabilityBench](https://arxiv.org/html/2601.06112v1)

### Inferences

All benefit and cost numbers in this section are my own estimates, based on the simulation in question 1 and a good run of 200-260 calls.

#### Summary table

| # | Measure | Failure it removes | Expected benefit | Extra model calls | Extra wall time | Work |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Cap each attempt at 20-30 s, one backup after about 8 s, cancel loser, max 3 rounds, SDK retries off | Hung calls eating the window (the 139-call run) | Model wait per agent at 6 % hangs: about 780 s down to about 270 s; no harm at 0 % | +5 to +16 % (10-40 calls) | none; saves minutes in bad runs | 1-1.5 h |
| 2 | One concurrency governor: semaphore of 28, hedges limited to 4 slots and 12 % of calls, agent steps before extraction | Self-inflicted queueing at the limit of 32; hedge storms | Removes one possible cause of hangs; keeps hedging safe | 0 | none | 30 min |
| 3 | Canary at start: 3 parallel one-token calls, first reply wins | "The very first call got no reply" | Saves up to 150 s at the start; gives a health reading | 3 | none (runs during browser start) | 15 min |
| 4 | Budget block after every step plus code-side step budgets per required item | Agents wandering; one item eating the window | In the source study: same accuracy at about 31 % lower cost; here mainly earlier finish | 0 (about 40 tokens per step) | none | 45 min |

#### Measure 1 and 2: bounded, hedged calls behind one governor

```python
import asyncio, collections, random, time

class Deadline:
    def __init__(self, seconds): self.t_end = time.monotonic() + seconds
    def left(self): return self.t_end - time.monotonic()

class LatencyStats:                              # one per call type: "step", "extract", "form"
    def __init__(self, default=8.0, lo=5.0, hi=12.0, n=60):
        self.buf = collections.deque(maxlen=n); self.default, self.lo, self.hi = default, lo, hi
    def add(self, s): self.buf.append(s)
    def hedge_delay(self):                       # rolling p90, clamped
        if len(self.buf) < 20: return self.default
        xs = sorted(self.buf)
        return min(self.hi, max(self.lo, xs[int(0.9 * (len(xs) - 1))]))

LLM_SLOTS   = asyncio.Semaphore(28)              # team limit is 32: keep headroom
HEDGE_SLOTS = asyncio.Semaphore(4)               # backups may never hold more than 4 slots

class HedgeBudget:                               # at most ~12 % extra calls
    def __init__(self): self.calls = 0; self.hedges = 0
    def primary(self): self.calls += 1
    def try_take(self):
        if self.hedges + 1 <= 0.12 * self.calls + 3: self.hedges += 1; return True
        return False
HEDGES = HedgeBudget()

class LLMUnavailable(Exception): pass

async def llm_call(make_request, *, kind, stats, deadline, cap=20.0, rounds=3, critical=False):
    """make_request() performs ONE HTTP call (client built with max_retries=0, timeout=cap+5).
    LLM calls have no side effects, so duplicates are safe; only the winner's action is executed."""
    for r in range(rounds):
        budget = min(cap, deadline.left() - 1.0)
        if budget < 2.0: break
        HEDGES.primary(); t0 = time.monotonic()

        async def primary():
            async with LLM_SLOTS: return await make_request()
        async def backup():
            async with HEDGE_SLOTS, LLM_SLOTS: return await make_request()

        tasks = [asyncio.create_task(primary())]
        try:
            wait_first = 0.0 if critical else min(stats[kind].hedge_delay(), budget)
            done, _ = await asyncio.wait(tasks, timeout=wait_first)
            if not done and HEDGES.try_take():                   # slow, not failed: add ONE backup, keep the primary
                tasks.append(asyncio.create_task(backup()))
            while True:
                good = [t for t in tasks if t.done() and not t.cancelled() and t.exception() is None]
                if good:
                    stats[kind].add(time.monotonic() - t0)
                    return good[0].result()
                pending = [t for t in tasks if not t.done()]
                left = budget - (time.monotonic() - t0)
                if not pending or left <= 0: break               # all failed, or round cap reached
                await asyncio.wait(pending, timeout=left, return_when=asyncio.FIRST_COMPLETED)
        finally:
            for t in tasks: t.cancel()                           # cancel the loser: closes the connection, frees the slot
            await asyncio.gather(*tasks, return_exceptions=True)
        await asyncio.sleep(random.random() * min(1.0, 0.25 * 2 ** r))   # short jittered pause
    raise LLMUnavailable(kind)
```

- Settings: `cap` 20 s for agent steps, 25-30 s for extraction calls with long output; `critical=True` (backup sent at once) only for the handful of calls on the path to the signature. Set `max_tokens` on every call.
- If the proxy streams: inside `make_request` wrap the first chunk in `asyncio.wait_for(first_chunk, 8)` and raise on expiry. A call with no first token after 8 s is treated as hung, while a long answer that is flowing is left alone.
- Priority: agent-step calls take `LLM_SLOTS` directly; the page-extraction fan-out should pass through a second, smaller semaphore (for example 16) so that a burst of pages can never starve the four agent loops.
- Circuit breaker for a proxy-wide bad day: if more than about 15 % of the last 20 calls hit the round cap, send agent-step calls to the fallback model through the metered proxy until 10 consecutive probe calls to the main model succeed. Cost: money only in bad runs.
- Cost check: at the default settings the simulation gives +10-16 % calls. With 4 loops and up to 16 extraction calls in flight, plus at most 4 backups, the peak is 24 concurrent calls, under the semaphore of 28.

#### Measure 3: canary

```python
async def canary(make_tiny_request, n=3, cap=10.0):
    tasks = [asyncio.create_task(make_tiny_request()) for _ in range(n)]     # max_tokens=1
    t0 = time.monotonic()
    done, pending = await asyncio.wait(tasks, timeout=cap, return_when=asyncio.FIRST_COMPLETED)
    for t in pending: t.cancel()
    return (time.monotonic() - t0) if done else None    # None -> start in degraded mode (fallback model, tighter budgets)
```

#### Measures 4 and 5: deadline controller and anytime bid

```python
RUN = Deadline(20 * 60)

def submit_reserve(stats):                       # recomputed during the run
    p90 = stats["form"].hedge_delay()            # live latency of this run
    est = FORM_BROWSER_SECONDS + FORM_LLM_CALLS * p90 * 1.5      # both constants from test-run logs
    return max(330.0, est)                       # floor: slowest submission seen in tests + 60-90 s; 480 s until measured

def investigation_left(stats): return RUN.left() - submit_reserve(stats)

def budget_block(agent, stats):                  # appended after every tool result
    left = investigation_left(stats); frac = left / INVESTIGATION_SECONDS
    tier = "HIGH" if frac >= .7 else "MEDIUM" if frac >= .3 else "LOW" if frac >= .1 else "CRITICAL"
    return (f"<budget>steps used {agent.steps}/{agent.max_steps}; investigation time left {int(left)} s; "
            f"tier {tier}; still missing: {', '.join(agent.missing()) or 'nothing'}. "
            f"LOW: finish the most valuable missing item only. CRITICAL: file what you have and stop.</budget>")

async def controller(agents, store, stats):
    while True:
        await asyncio.sleep(2)
        if store.changed(): store.bid = compute_bid(store.records)          # deterministic; always a submittable bid
        if store.checklist_complete() and store.verified(): break           # early stop: all required records present
        if investigation_left(stats) <= 0: break                            # hard cut-off
    for a in agents: a.cancel()
    await submit_and_sign(store.bid, deadline=RUN)                          # calls here use critical=True
```

- The model still chooses every navigation step; code only tells it the time, enforces the stop, and computes the bid.
- Per-item step budgets: when an item on an agent's list has used its allowance (for example 12 steps), mark it unresolved in the block and require the agent to move to the next item.
- If the form allows it, open and pre-fill it in a second browser context once the first complete draft bid exists, so that only the final update and the signature remain after the cut-off.

#### Measure 6: supervisor with clean restart

```python
STARTS = ["navigate from the home page", "use the site search first", "start from the sitemap or footer links"]

async def supervise(site, make_agent, store, stats, stall_s=75, max_restarts=2):
    for attempt in range(max_restarts + 1):
        if investigation_left(stats) < 60 or store.site_complete(site): return
        agent = make_agent(site, start_hint=STARTS[attempt % len(STARTS)],
                           summary=store.summary(site))        # built by code: records filed, URLs visited, dead ends
        task = asyncio.create_task(agent.run(store))           # fresh context: the old transcript is dropped
        while not task.done():
            await asyncio.wait([task], timeout=5)
            stalled = time.monotonic() - store.last_progress(site) > stall_s   # no new record or filed page
            looping = agent.same_action_repeats() >= 3                          # same tool+arguments or same URL
            if stalled or looping or investigation_left(stats) <= 0:
                task.cancel(); break
        await asyncio.gather(task, return_exceptions=True)
```

- Set `stall_s` from logs: the longest gap between two filed pages in the runs that scored 100, times 1.5.
- Work stealing: when a site finishes early, call `supervise` a second time for the site with the most missing items, with a different start hint; both agents write to the same store. This uses slots that would otherwise sit idle.
- The store and the visited set are written at every step and flushed to disk at each stage, so a restart or crash loses nothing.

#### Measure 7: redundancy only where it pays

- Deterministic validation first, at no model cost: types, ranges, units, currency, totals across records, and required fields present. A failed check sends the page back to extraction once with the error named.
- Dual extraction for pages whose records feed the bid: second call with a different view of the page (structured table text versus raw text, or reversed section order) at the same time as the first; compare field by field in code; only disagreeing fields get a third opinion (frontier model through the metered proxy if a wrong value would cost more than the call).
- Decision-model gates, each a short call: "does this page contain a record of type X" before a document is filed or dropped, and "is every item on this checklist supported by a filed page" before an agent may declare itself done.
- No voting on ordinary navigation steps.

#### Measure 8: measurement in few runs

- Log one line per attempt: call type, start time, first-token time, total time, output tokens, outcome (ok, capped, backup won, cancelled), calls in flight. Log one line per stage with success and duration, and the slack in seconds at the cut-off and at the signature.
- Replay: store every filed page of a good run; run extraction and bid computation on the stored set 20 times and report per-field agreement and bid agreement. This is the stage-level pass^k.
- Fault injection wrapper around `make_request` for test runs: with probability 6 % sleep for 300 s (a hang), with probability 10 % multiply latency by 3, and once per run stall a whole agent for 90 s. Acceptance test before the final: three consecutive fault-injected runs that all sign a complete bid. Three runs cannot prove 95 % reliability (see question 2), but a fault-injected pass shows the two known failure modes are handled.
- For the final evaluation: make sure no other run of the team is active, since the 32-call limit is shared across runs.

### Gaps
- All benefit figures here are estimates from a simulation with an assumed lognormal latency and independent hangs; real hangs may cluster in time, which lowers the benefit of hedging and raises the value of the fallback route.
- `FORM_BROWSER_SECONDS`, `FORM_LLM_CALLS`, the stall threshold and the number of bid-relevant pages must be read from the team's own run logs; I had no access to them.
- Whether dual extraction, the decision-model gates and work stealing stay within the challenge's fair-play rules is for the team to confirm against the rules text; they keep the model in charge of navigation, searches and document choice, which is the constraint stated in the brief.
- None of the measures has been tested on this code base; the pseudocode is unexecuted and should be run under the fault-injection wrapper before it is trusted.

# Reliability engineering and variance reduction for deadline-bound LLM agent systems (as of October 2026)

Reading notes for the writer:
- "Task brief" means the numbers supplied with the assignment (scores 100, 100, 100, 44.9, 38.2, 15, 10; p50 3 s, p95 9 s; 32 concurrent calls; 120-150 s client wait; 200-260 calls in a good run; 139 calls and 9 unanswered calls in one bad run).
- "Own estimate" marks numbers I computed myself (a lognormal fit to p50 = 3 s / p95 = 9 s, a Monte Carlo simulation of one agent loop, exact binomial calculations). They are not from a source.
- "Background" marks classic systems sources. "Search summary only" marks papers whose numbers I took from a search-result summary without reading the full text; treat those as leads to verify.

## 1. Tail latency: what do hedged requests, tied requests, adaptive timeouts and retry budgets recommend, and what timeout and hedge delay fit a call with p50 = 3 s and p95 = 9 s?

### Takeaway
The measured failure (9 calls unanswered for 120-150 s) is a hang problem, and the fix with by far the largest effect is a short per-attempt cap (about 20 s) plus one backup request after roughly the p90-p95 of observed latency (7-9 s), with the loser cancelled. By my simulation this brings one agent's model-wait time at a 6 % hang rate from about 780 s back to about 270 s, for 10-16 % extra calls.

### Cited Findings
- Background. Fan-out amplifies rare slowness: if one server is slow 1 time in 100, a request that touches 100 servers is slow 63 % of the time. — [The Tail at Scale, summary by The Morning Paper](https://blog.acolyer.org/2015/01/15/the-tail-at-scale/)
- Background. Hedged request: send the same request again only after the first has been outstanding longer than the 95th-percentile expected latency "for this class of requests", then use whichever answers first; this limits extra load to about 5 %. — [Dean and Barroso 2013, CACM](https://cacm.acm.org/research/the-tail-at-scale/); [summary](https://blog.acolyer.org/2015/01/15/the-tail-at-scale/)
- Background. Google's BigTable benchmark (1,000 keys over 100 servers): a hedge after 10 ms cut the 99.9th-percentile latency from 1,800 ms to 74 ms with 2 % more requests. Quoted from memory of the paper; the CACM page returned HTTP 403 in this session, so verify before printing. — [Dean and Barroso 2013, CACM](https://cacm.acm.org/research/the-tail-at-scale/)
- Background. Tied requests: enqueue on two servers at once and let each cancel the other when one starts work; in a real Google system the median fell 16 % and the 99.9th percentile fell 40 %. This needs server-side cross-cancellation. — [summary](https://blog.acolyer.org/2015/01/15/the-tail-at-scale/)
- Background. Other techniques in the same paper: "good enough" results (return once enough of the fan-out has answered), canary requests (send to one or two servers first to catch a request or backend that stalls), and latency-induced probation (stop sending to a slow machine, keep probing it, readmit it when it recovers). — [summary](https://blog.acolyer.org/2015/01/15/the-tail-at-scale/)
- Background. Google SRE retry rules: a request is attempted at most three times; a client only retries while its retries are under 10 % of its requests. Without the per-client budget worst-case load grows about 3x, with it about 1.1x. Retries should happen at one layer only, to avoid a combinatorial retry explosion. — [Google SRE book, Handling Overload](https://sre.google/sre-book/handling-overload/)
- Background. Client-side adaptive throttling: track requests and accepts over two minutes, and start rejecting locally once requests exceed K times accepts (K = 2 preferred). Requests carry a criticality (CRITICAL_PLUS, CRITICAL, SHEDDABLE_PLUS, SHEDDABLE), and lower criticalities are shed first. — [Google SRE book, Handling Overload](https://sre.google/sre-book/handling-overload/)
- LLM-specific, 2026. A typical LLM call is described as p50 about 8 s and p95 about 18 s; "A retry policy designed for 50ms RPCs does not survive contact with an 8-second LLM call." The author recommends hedging when the primary exceeds its measured p90 (or p95 for cross-provider failover), a hedge budget capped at 5-10 % of base traffic, a global retry cap of 5-15 %, and separate budgets for timeouts versus errors. — [Tian Pan, May 2026](https://tianpan.co/blog/2026/05/02/tail-tolerant-retry-policy-llm-gateway-latency-cliff)
- Same source: with a 10 s per-attempt timeout, 1 s backoff and three sequential retries, a model p99 of 18 s turns into a caller-visible p99 of about 33 s; sequential failover across three providers can add 30 s. Hedging gives min(primary, hedge) where retrying gives primary + retry. The outcome claims in this post are the author's estimates, not measurements. — [Tian Pan, May 2026](https://tianpan.co/blog/2026/05/02/tail-tolerant-retry-policy-llm-gateway-latency-cliff)
- Adaptive hedging in a simulation of 50,000 requests with 5 % stragglers at 10x latency: hedging at the observed p90 (tracked with a quantile sketch over 30-60 s windows) cut p99 from 65.0 ms to 17.3 ms (about 74 %) for 8.9 % extra requests, with p50 unchanged. A static hedge at 10 ms gave 17.5 ms for 7.7 % overhead; a static hedge at 50 ms gave 54.9 ms for 2.1 %. The library was not in production; these are simulation numbers. — [InfoQ, adaptive hedged requests](https://www.infoq.com/articles/adaptive-hedged-requests-p99-latency/)
- Same source, on LLM inference: streaming endpoints return HTTP headers in 1-2 ms, so the hedge timer must run on time to first token, not on time to first byte. Calibrated on first byte the hedger fired on almost every call (about 100 % overhead); calibrated on first token the overhead was 17-19.8 %. — [InfoQ](https://www.infoq.com/articles/adaptive-hedged-requests-p99-latency/)
- Same source, when not to hedge: non-idempotent requests; a single-instance backend (the hedge lands on the same slow machine); CPU-saturated backends; services under about 1 request per second (too little data for the sketch); and services behind a shared rate limit, where a 20 % hedge rate could itself trigger throttling. — [InfoQ](https://www.infoq.com/articles/adaptive-hedged-requests-p99-latency/)
- A hedge budget of 10 % as a token bucket empties in about one second during a full outage, so hedging stops before it doubles backend load. — [InfoQ](https://www.infoq.com/articles/adaptive-hedged-requests-p99-latency/)
- An open-source hedging library aimed at LLM inference claims a 75-96 % p99 reduction for 5-10 % cost overhead and offers fixed, percentile, adaptive and "workload-aware" (prompt length, model complexity) delay strategies with `max_hedges: 1` and loser cancellation. README claim, not independently verified. — [crucible_hedging README](https://github.com/North-Shore-AI/crucible_hedging)
- Cost framing: hedging at p95 means "paying twice for 5% of requests". — [dev.to, Request Hedging](https://dev.to/gabrielanhaia/request-hedging-the-tail-at-scale-technique-most-teams-skip-2j37)
- The OpenAI Python client waits 10 minutes by default and retries twice by default, so a wrapper that owns timeouts and retries should set `timeout=` and `max_retries=0` explicitly. Cited from memory of the README, not re-fetched in this session. — [openai-python README](https://github.com/openai/openai-python)

### Inferences
- Own estimate. A lognormal distribution through p50 = 3 s and p95 = 9 s has p75 = 4.7 s, p90 = 7.1 s, p99 = 14.2 s and p99.9 = 23.6 s. Under it, P(latency > 12 s) = 1.9 %, P(> 20 s) = 0.23 %, P(> 30 s) = 0.03 %. A healthy call essentially never needs more than 25-30 s, so a wait of 120-150 s buys nothing: a call that has not answered by about 20 s is hung, not slow.
- Own estimate. The latency is therefore a mixture: a normal body plus a "no reply" mass. In the bad run it was 9 of about 148 attempts, roughly 6 %. With 260 calls per run, even a 1 % hang rate gives a 93 % chance of at least one hang per run (1 - 0.99^260), and each hang costs one agent 120-150 s, which is 30-40 normal calls. This is the same arithmetic as the 63 % fan-out example.
- Own estimate, Monte Carlo of one agent loop of 65 sequential calls (seconds of model wait: median / p95; extra calls):

| Policy | hang 0 % | hang 1 % | hang 3 % | hang 6 % | extra calls at 6 % |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| wait 135 s, then retry (today) | 242 / 283 | 283 / 531 | 504 / 898 | 782 / 1317 | +6 % |
| cap 30 s, then retry | 243 / 283 | 260 / 324 | 299 / 390 | 363 / 481 | +6 % |
| cap 20 s, then retry | 242 / 282 | 254 / 305 | 282 / 350 | 325 / 413 | +7 % |
| cap 12 s, then retry | 243 / 283 | 250 / 295 | 267 / 317 | 292 / 354 | +8 % (kills 2 % of healthy calls) |
| hedge at 9 s, round cap 25 s | 239 / 275 | 245 / 280 | 256 / 300 | 277 / 328 | +11 % |
| hedge at 7 s, round cap 20 s | 235 / 267 | 240 / 274 | 250 / 289 | 266 / 312 | +16 % |
| hedge at 5 s, round cap 20 s | 228 / 257 | 232 / 262 | 239 / 273 | 252 / 292 | +27 % |

- Reading of the table: almost all of the gain comes from shortening the cap (782 s to 325 s at a 6 % hang rate). Hedging adds a further 15-20 % and, unlike a very short cap, does not throw away a primary that is slow but alive. Moving the hedge from 9 s to 5 s buys little and more than doubles the overhead.
- Recommended starting values for this system (own estimate): connect timeout 5 s; hedge after 8 s, then adaptive at the rolling p90 of the last 50-60 completions of that call type, clamped to 5-12 s; per-round cap 20 s for agent steps and 25-30 s for long-output extraction calls; at most one backup; at most three rounds; SDK retries off. If streaming works through the proxy, trigger the hedge on "no first token after 6-8 s", which separates a hung call from a long answer.
- Timeouts tuned to output length: completion time is roughly time-to-first-token plus output tokens divided by tokens per second, so set the cap per call type from logged data (cap = p99 of first-token time + max_tokens / slow-case token rate) and set `max_tokens` on every call so the bound is real. I found no source giving a formula; this is a reasoned rule.
- Cost under the cap of 32: a hedge occupies one extra slot for at most the remainder of the round (about 12 s). With four agent loops plus a page-extraction fan-out, a hedge budget of 10-15 % of calls and at most 4 slots for hedges keeps the system below 32. More important, a short cap frees slots: under today's policy 9 hung calls each held a slot for 2 minutes.
- Hedging does not help if hangs come from the team's own traffic exceeding the 32-call limit (requests queued at the proxy). Then extra requests make it worse, as the "shared rate limit" warning says. A client-side semaphore below 32 rules that cause out; no second run of the team should be active during the final evaluation because the limit is shared across runs.
- The hung calls in the bad run looked independent per request (9 of about 148 failed while the rest of the run continued), which is the case hedging handles. If the whole proxy degrades, hedging to the same proxy cannot help; a fallback route to another model through the metered proxy can.
- Canary requests map directly onto "the very first call got no reply": send 2-3 one-token calls in parallel at start-up and use the first that returns as both warm-up and health probe.

### Gaps
- No published latency distribution for Qwen3.8-Flash-Next through this proxy; all percentiles beyond p50 and p95 are from my lognormal fit. Whether the proxy supports streaming, and the first-token distribution, are unknown.
- Unknown whether cancelling a request client-side makes the proxy stop generation and release the concurrency slot. If it does not, cancelled losers still count against the 32 for a while. This can be tested in ten minutes by cancelling 20 calls and watching whether 32 fresh ones are admitted.
- I found no measured, peer-reviewed study of hedging LLM API calls; the LLM-specific sources are engineering posts and one simulation.
- Whether the 9 unanswered calls were proxy-side hangs, queueing behind the team's own concurrency, or dropped connections is not known; it decides how much hedging helps versus a plain short cap.

## 2. Variance and reliability measurement: pass^k, "AI Agents That Matter", HAL, temperature-0 variance studies; how many runs separate 80 % from 95 %, and what cheap proxies exist?

### Takeaway
Agent systems that succeed most of the time still fail on a large share of repeated trials, and full runs are far too expensive to measure this: about 30 full runs are needed to tell 80 % from 95 % reliability, so the team has to measure per call and per stage, on saved pages and with injected faults.
